Check page history in case this page was moved, since the everybodywiki page may have been under a different title[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 20:10, 11 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Miwa Shrine | image = [[File:Miwa shrine №2 Fuefuki-city.JPG|250px]]
Haiden of Miwa Shrine | location = 1450-1 Ninomiya, Misaka-cho, Fuefuki City, Yamanashi Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|35|37|47.74|N|138|39|12.84|E|region:JP-19|display=inline,title}} | deity = {{ill|Ōmononushi|ja|大物主命|lt=Ōmononushi no Mikoto|12=draft}} | type = Kokushi Genzaisha (Shinto shrine listed in historical records), Ninomiya of Kai Province, Former Prefectural Shrine | established = Traditionally attributed to the era of Emperor Keikō | honden_style = Nagare-zukuri | festival = March 15 | rituals = Yutate Ritual (February 8) | map = {{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=13|frame-align=center|frame-width=200}} }} {{ill|Miwa Shrine (Fuefuki City)|ja|美和神社 (笛吹市)|lt=Miwa Shrine|12=draft}} (美和神社) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in [[Japan]]. It is a [[Ninomiya (shrine)|Ninomiya]], or a second rank shrine in its province after the [[Ichinomiya]]. [[File:Miwa shrine Fuefuki-city.JPG|thumb|250px|Torii at Miwa Shrine (photo taken in April 2010)]] '''Misode Tenmangū''' (御袖天満宮) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社|12=draft}} ({{ill|Tenman-gū|ja|天満宮|12=draft}}) located in {{ill|Onomichi, Hiroshima|ja|尾道市|12=draft}}, {{ill|Hiroshima Prefecture|ja|広島県|12=draft}}. The shrine's former ranking was {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社|12=draft}}. == Enshrined deity == The shrine enshrines {{ill|Sugawara no Michizane|ja|Sugawara no Michizane|12=draft}}, also known as Tenjin. == History == In the first year of {{ill|Engi|ja|延喜|12=draft}} ({{ill|901|ja|901st year|12=draft}}), the deity, during his lifetime, was exiled to {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府|12=draft}} due to slander by {{ill|Fujiwara no Tokihira|ja|藤原時平|12=draft}}. While traveling by ship, he landed at Onomichi, where locals served him barley rice and {{ill|reishu|ja|醴酒|12=draft}}. In gratitude, he tore a sleeve from his {{ill|kimono|ja|和服|12=draft}} and used it to depict his image, which he left with the locals. After his death (in the third year of Engi, 903), a small shrine was established during the {{ill|Enkyū|ja|延久|12=draft}} era (1069–1074) within the grounds of the temple Tenjinbō, to enshrine the "image on the sleeve," thus giving the shrine its name, Misode Tenmangū.{{Sfn|Shinto Encyclopedia|1936}} Tenjinbō later became {{ill|Ōyamadera|ja|大山寺|12=draft}} and served as the shrine's {{ill|bettō|ja|別当寺|12=draft}} until the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離|12=draft}} reforms of the {{ill|Meiji era|ja|明治時代|12=draft}}. It remains adjacent to the shrine today. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ja|近代社格制度|1=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|12=draft}}, the shrine was classified as a gōsha. There are numerous legends about Sugawara no Michizane's stops along the Seto Inland Sea in the {{ill|Chūgoku region|ja|中国地方|12=draft}}, with one version stating that a person named Kanaya hosted him. Some researchers suggest that the wealthy Kanaya family may have incorporated this narrative to emphasize their status. During the {{ill|Edo period|ja|江戸時代|12=draft}}, particularly the early 19th century, the Kanaya family accumulated wealth from the thriving {{ill|Onomichi Port|ja|尾道港|12=draft}}. They commissioned noted scholars such as {{ill|Rai Sanyō|ja|頼山陽|12=draft}} and {{ill|Kan Chazan|ja|菅茶山|12=draft}} to write commemorative inscriptions for the shrine. The family also maintained barley fields used to brew reishu for the deity's reception. The family eventually disappeared, and the fields became overgrown by the mid-20th century.{{Sfn|Hiroshima Encyclopedia|1982}} == Festivals and Rituals == [[File:Miwa-shrine Yutateshinji Kagura.JPG|thumb|250px|Prayer dance during the Yutate ritual (photo taken on February 8, 2011)]] The "Tenjin Festival" is held over three days in mid-July (the weekend preceding July 25). Events include: - **Day 1:** A {{ill|mikoshi|ja|神輿|12=draft}} procession. - **Day 2:** Educational ceremonies, raffles, and entertainment performances. - **Day 3:** A concluding ceremony featuring the mikoshi ascending and descending the shrine's 55 stone steps during the "55-Step Daishinden Return Ceremony." == Shrine Buildings == The {{ill|honden|ja|本殿|12=draft}} is constructed in an {{ill|irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造|12=draft}} style with copper roofing. The original structure was destroyed in a fire in {{ill|Shōwa 48 (1973)|ja|昭和48th year|12=draft}} and rebuilt in {{ill|Shōwa 58 (1983)|ja|昭和58th year|12=draft}}. The {{ill|haiden|ja|拝殿|12=draft}} also features irimoya-zukuri construction, and the main gate ({{ill|Shinmon|ja|神門|12=draft}}) is an eight-legged gate (hakkaku-mon) in a {{ill|kirizuma-zukuri|ja|切妻造|12=draft}} style. == Grounds == The shrine's approach features 55 stone steps crafted from single slabs, with the last step intentionally joined from smaller stones. Nearby is a "resting stone" where the deity reportedly rested and a {{ill|sasuri-ushi|ja|さすり牛|12=draft}}, a rubbing ox statue believed to grant blessings. The shrine has been featured in various media. The steps were prominently shown in the film ''{{ill|Tenkōsei|ja|転校生 (映画)|12=draft}}'' and the drama ''{{ill|Teppan|ja|てっぱん|12=draft}}.'' The shrine grounds inspired the setting for ''{{ill|Kamisama no Memo-chō|ja|かみちゅ!|12=draft}},'' although its structures were modeled after {{ill|Ushitora Shrine|ja|艮神社|12=draft}} in the same city. == Access == - A 20-minute walk from {{ill|Onomichi Station|ja|尾道駅|12=draft}} on the {{ill|San'yō Main Line|ja|山陽本線|12=draft}}. - A 5-minute walk from the "Nagasaiguchi" bus stop served by {{ill|Onomichi Bus|ja|おのみちバス|12=draft}} and {{ill|Chūgoku Bus|ja|中国バス|12=draft}}. - A 5-minute walk from the {{ill|Senkoji Ropeway|ja|千光寺山ロープウェイ|12=draft}} lower station. == Related Articles == * {{ill|Seichi junrei|ja|巡礼 (通俗)|12=draft}} * {{ill|Ōyamadera|ja|大山寺 (尾道市)|12=draft}} == References == {{reflist}} == Bibliography == * ''Hiroshima Encyclopedia'' (広島県大百科事典〈下巻〉). Chūgoku Shimbun, 1982. == External Links == * [http://misodetenmangu.or.jp/ Official website of Misode Tenmangū] {{Shinto pilgrimage}} {{Shinto-stub}} {{commonscat|Miwa-jinja, Fuefuki}} {{citation needed|Miwa Shrine Fuefuki}} {{shinto-stub}} {{Draft categories| }} {{Miwa and Yamato Faith}} {{draft categories| }} {{⚠️🚨COPIED from EverybodyWiki ❗❕⚠️😡😤Please respect Licence CC-BY-SA ❗}} {{Source Wikipedia}} {{afc comment|1=see [[every:Miwa Shrine (Fuefuki City)]] for the history[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 02:25, 31 March 2025 (UTC)}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Shinto shrines in Hiroshima]] [[Category:Tenman-gū shrines]] [[Category:Former Gōsha shrines]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Onomichi]] [[Category:History of Onomichi]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Yamanashi Prefecture]] [[Category:History of Fuefuki City]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Fuefuki City]] [[Category:Kokushi Genzaisha]] [[Category:Prefectural shrines in Yamanashi Prefecture]] [[Category:Kai Province shrines]] [[Category:Cultural Properties of Japan]] [[Category:Intangible Cultural Heritage of Japan]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Japan]] [[Category:Miwa shrines]] [[Category:Miwa Shrine (Fuefuki City)]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:11]] [[Category: Completion tier 2]] [[Category:New-]] [[Category:Pages from everybodywiki under right title]] [[Category:New]] [[Category:completion tier 2]] }} [[en:draft:Miwa Shrine (Fuefuki City)]] [[ja:美和神社 (笛吹市)]] [[ja:御袖天満宮]] [[sn:Miwa Shrine (Fuefuki City)]] {{神社 |name = Miwa Shrine (美和神社) |image = [[File:Miwa shrine №2 Fuefuki-city.JPG|250px]]
Miwa Shrine Haiden (美和神社 拝殿) |religious_affiliation = {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道|12=draft}} |location = {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|ja|山梨県|12=draft}}{{ill|Fuefuki City|ja|笛吹市|12=draft}}{{ill|Misaka Town|ja|御坂町|12=draft}}{{ill|Ninomiya|ja|二之宮|12=draft}}1450-1 |coordinates = {{coord|35|37|47.74|N|138|39|12.84|E|region:JP-19|display=inline,title}} |deity = {{ill|Ōmononushi|ja|大物主神|12=draft}} |type = {{ill|Kokushi-Minaisha|ja|国史見在社|12=draft}}
{{ill|Kai Province|ja|甲斐国|12=draft}}{{ill|First Shrine|ja|一宮|lt=Second Shrine|lt_ja=二宮|12=draft}}
Former {{ill|Prefectural Shrine|ja|県社|12=draft}} |foundation = (trad.) Period of {{ill|Emperor Keikō|ja|景行天皇|12=draft}} |main_shrine = {{ill|Nagare-zukuri|ja|流造|12=draft}} |alternative_names = |subsidiary = |festival = {{ill|March 15|ja|3月15日|12=draft}} |ritual = Yudate Ritual (February 8) |map = {{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=13|frame-align=center|frame-width=200}} }} [[File:Miwa shrine Fuefuki-city.JPG|thumb|250px|Miwa Shrine Torii (Photographed April 2010)]] '''Miwa Shrine''' (美和神社) is a {{ill|Shrine|ja|神社|12=draft}} located in {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|ja|山梨県|12=draft}} {{ill|Fuefuki City|ja|笛吹市|12=draft}}. It is a {{ill|Kokushi-Minaisha|ja|国史見在社|12=draft}}, and in {{ill|Kai Province|ja|甲斐国|12=draft}} it is known as {{ill|First Shrine|ja|一宮|lt=Second Shrine|lt_ja=二宮|12=draft}}, with its former shrine rank being {{ill|Prefectural Shrine|ja|県社|12=draft}}. == Deity == * {{ill|Ōmononushi|ja|大物主神|12=draft}} (Oomononushi-no-Kami) == Location == Miwa Shrine is situated in the eastern part of the {{ill|Kofu Basin|ja|甲府盆地|12=draft}} and enshrined in the Ninomiya district of the northwestern area. In ancient Kai Province, the early provincial capital ({{ill|Provincial Capital|ja|国府|12=draft}}) was located in {{ill|Kasuga Town, Fuefuki City|ja|笛吹市春日居町|12=draft}}, at the north-central edge of the basin, and is believed to have later been relocated to the vicinity of the national government office in {{ill|Misaka Town, Fuefuki City|ja|笛吹市御坂町|12=draft}}. The Misaka area is dotted with small to medium-sized burial mounds from the Kofun period—such as the {{ill|Kamekōdzuka Tumulus|ja|亀甲塚古墳|12=draft}} and {{ill|Baba Tumulus|ja|姥塚古墳|12=draft}}—as well as settlement ruins like the {{ill|Ninomiya Ruins|ja|二之宮遺跡|12=draft}}, and in ancient times, various governmental ruins and historic sites were spread throughout the area. Under the Ritsuryō system, the area was equated with Inoue Village in Yamanashi District, and the name “Ninomiya” is derived from its proximity to the national administrative office and Miwa Shrine. In the early modern period, Ninomiya Village was established, centered around Miwa Shrine. The shrine, located in the Ninomiya district, is designated as {{ill|Satomiya|ja|里宮|12=draft}}, while in the Oyama area to the east of Ninomiya stands {{ill|Yamamiya|ja|山宮|12=draft}} in the form of {{ill|Kinegami Shrine|ja|杵衡神社|12=draft}}. == History == It is generally believed that Miwa Shrine was enshrined by being invited from {{ill|Ōmiya Shrine|ja|大神神社|12=draft}} of {{ill|Yamato Province|ja|Yamato Province|12=draft}} ({{ill|Nara Prefecture|ja|奈良県|12=draft}}), which regards {{ill|Mount Miwa|ja|三輪山|12=draft}} as its shintai, and that after being transferred to the {{ill|Kinegami Shrine|ja|杵衡神社|12=draft}} in Onoe Village, it was newly relocated to Ninomiya. According to the texts “{{ill|Kai Kokashiki-ji|ja|甲斐国社記・寺記|12=draft}}” and “{{ill|Kai Kokushi|ja|甲斐国志|12=draft}}”, the shrine’s origins are said to date back to the time of {{ill|Emperor Keikō|ja|景行天皇|12=draft}}, when the provincial governor of Kai ({{ill|Provincial Governor of Kai|ja|甲斐国造|12=draft}}) and {{ill|Shio-umi Ashin|ja|塩海足尼|12=draft}} performed the enshrinement. The earliest historical record appears in an entry of “{{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|ja|日本三代実録|12=draft}}” dated June 8, [[863]] ({{ill|Jōgan era|ja|Jōgan|12=draft}} 5), which states that on that day Miwa Shrine was conferred the junior fifth rank and granted the title “Ninomiya” by {{ill|Emperor Ichijō|ja|一条天皇|12=draft}}. In the medieval period, it received veneration from the {{ill|Takeda clan|ja|武田氏|12=draft}}—the guardians of Kai—and in [[1479]] ({{ill|Bunmei era|ja|Bunmei|12=draft}} 11) the lord of {{ill|Shinano Province|ja|信濃国|12=draft}}’s {{ill|Saku District|ja|佐久郡|12=draft}}, the {{ill|Ōi clan|ja|大井氏|12=draft}}, invaded Kai; during this time Miwa Shrine also suffered from warfare. In the period of {{ill|Takeda Shigetora|ja|武田信虎|12=draft}}, the shrine was granted estates in {{ill|Manriki Village|ja|万力郷|12=draft}} in {{ill|Yamanashi District|ja|山梨郡|12=draft}} (present-day {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|ja|山梨県|12=draft}}), and in [[1557]] ({{ill|Kōji era|ja|Kōji (Muromachi period)|lt=Kōji|lt_ja=Kōji|12=draft}} 3) it received a charter from {{ill|Takeda Shingen|ja|武田信玄|lt=Takeda Harunobu|lt_ja=武田晴信|12=draft}} (Shingen), alongside {{ill|Asama Shrine (Fuefuki City)|ja|浅間神社 (笛吹市)|lt=Asama Shrine|lt_ja=浅間神社|12=draft}} (located in Ichinomiya, Ichinomiya Town, Fuefuki City), {{ill|Tamamoro Shrine|ja|玉諸神社|lt=Tamamoro Shrine|lt_ja=玉諸神社|12=draft}} in Kōfu City, and the Takeda clan’s tutelary shrine, {{ill|Takeda Hachiman Shrine|ja|武田八幡宮|12=draft}} (in {{ill|Nirasaki City|ja|韮崎市|12=draft}}), among others—exempting them from serving at Fuchū Hachiman Shrine (currently {{ill|Hachiman Shrine (Kōfu)|ja|八幡神社 (甲府市宮前町)|12=draft}} in Kōfu City). In June [[1565]] (Eiroku 8) a {{ill|Tachi (sword)|ja|太刀|12=draft}} offering was made by a retainer of {{ill|Takeda Yoshinobu|ja|武田義信|12=draft}}, the heir of the Takeda family, as recorded in the Miwa Shrine document “Kōshū Ninomiya Zōritchō”. According to “{{ill|Kōyō Gunkan|ja|甲陽軍鑑|12=draft}}”, in January of the preceding year [[1564]] (Eirōku 7) a retainer of Yoshinobu was punished for attempting a rebellion, and in the following year, [[1565]] (Eirōku 8), an incident occurred in which Yoshinobu himself was confined; however, from the records of the Zōritchō it is thought that the incident was uncovered in 1565 (Eirōku 8). Furthermore, in the following year [[1566]] (Eirōku 9), {{ill|Sanjō Consort|ja|三条夫人|12=draft}}—who was also the mother of Yoshinobu—offered armaments ({{ill|Armor|ja|具足|12=draft}}). On September 11, [[1573]] ({{ill|Genki era|ja|元亀|12=draft}} 4) immediately after the succession, {{ill|Takeda Katsuyori|ja|武田勝頼|12=draft}} ordered a prayer for enduring military fortune, and in [[1579]] ({{ill|Tenshō era|ja|天正|1=Tenshō (Momoyama period)|lt=Tenshō Era|12=draft}} 7) he imposed a prohibition. After the fall of the Takeda clan, in [[1582]] (Tenshō 10) prohibitions were issued by {{ill|Oda Nobunaga|ja|織田信長|12=draft}} and {{ill|Oda Nobutada|ja|織田信忠|12=draft}}, and in the following year [[1583]] (Tenshō 11) the shrine received a guarantee for its estates from {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|ja|徳川家康|12=draft}}, with the estates finally confirmed in [[1589]] (Tenshō 17) by a land survey conducted by {{ill|Inatadashi|ja|伊奈忠次|12=draft}}. During the era of Toyotomi-affiliated daimyō, the shrine received donations of estates from {{ill|Kato Mitsuyasu|ja|加藤光泰|12=draft}} and the {{ill|Asano clan|ja|浅野氏|12=draft}}. As a ritual, from the Sengoku period through early modern times a joint pilgrimage—known as the “Three-Shrine Onmiyuki”—was mandated. This ritual, performed at the Shingen Embankment ({{ill|Shingen Embankment|ja|信玄堤|12=draft}}) in {{ill|Kai City|ja|甲斐市|12=draft}}, involved the three shrines of Ichinomiya and Sannomiya; the summer onmiyuki was held on the third Ino day in April, and the winter onmiyuki on the second Ino day in November. During the Meiji period, with the prohibition of the three-shrine pilgrimage, the Yamamiya Onmiyuki (the Ninomiya Onmiyuki), which had been held on the first day of March, was rescheduled to April 15 and designated as the spring festival; although this event was interrupted for a time in the postwar era, it is now held on the first Sunday of April with the Taitei Kagura offered in dedication. Also, every February 8 the {{ill|Yudate Ritual|ja|湯立神事|12=draft}} is observed. Miwa Shrine’s Yudate Ritual, which is accompanied by the prayer dance of Sarutahiko, is the only surviving Yudate Ritual in the prefecture. According to a locally handed‐down document from 1826 (Bunsei 9), the Ninomiya Yudate was held separately on February 8—distinct from the Taitei Kagura held in mid‐March—and the dance of Sarutahiko is also recorded in {{ill|Uramihankuwa|ja|裏見寒話|12=draft}}. The shrine priesthood is provided by the Sakanai family, and {{ill|Sakanai Sōō|ja|坂名井聡翁|12=draft}} is known as a Kokugaku scholar. == Cultural Properties, etc. == [[File:Miwa-shrine Yutateshinji Kagura.JPG|thumb|250px|Prayer Dance of Sarutahiko during the Yudate Ritual (Photographed February 8, 2011)]] [[File:Miwa-shrine Yutateshinji A.JPG|thumb|250px|Ritual during the Yudate Ritual (Photographed February 8, 2011)]] [[File:Miwa-shrine Yutateshinji B.JPG|thumb|250px|Soaking bamboo leaves in boiling water and pouring it on worshippers (Photographed February 8, 2011)]] ; Important Cultural Properties (National Designation) * Sculpture ** Wooden Standing Statue of Ōmononushi – designated in [[1906]] (Meiji 39) on September 6; a work from the Heian period{{National Designated Cultural Properties Database|201|2937|Wooden Standing Statue of Ōmononushi}} (accessed May 19, 2017){{PDFlink|[https://www.city.fuefuki.yamanashi.jp/documents/607/5bf21d9faea4d.pdf Fuefuki City Cultural Properties Guidebook]}} – Fuefuki City, accessed December 23, 2019. ; Designated Tangible Cultural Properties of Yamanashi Prefecture * Crafts ** White Thread-Tied Armor (fragmentary) – designated in [[1986]] (Showa 61) on March 19; a work from the Nanboku-chō period{{Refnest|group="Notes"|Armor researcher Ichirō Miura has estimated, based on its manufacturing technique, that this armor dates from the period of {{ill|Takeda Nobunari|ja|武田信成|12=draft}} and {{ill|Takeda Nobuharu|ja|武田信春|lt=Nobuharu|lt_ja=信春|12=draft}}.Ichirō Miura, ''Resurrecting the Takeda Army: Its Armor and Military Attire'', Miyabari Publishing, May 28, 2007, pp. 7–13}} ** Vermilion Talisman and Red Thread Unarmored Armor with Accompanying Targe – designated in 1986 (Showa 61) on March 19; a legendary coming-of-age armor of {{ill|Takeda Shingen|ja|武田信玄|lt=Takeda Harunobu|lt_ja=武田晴信|12=draft}}{{Refnest|group="Notes"|However, Ichirō Miura notes that from its style this armor is a work of the Tenshō period—later than the time of Shingen’s coming-of-age—and that its manufacturing technique and design share commonalities with the armors of military commanders active under the Oda–Toyotomi regime (such as the gold small-talisman white thread unarmored armor of {{ill|Maeda Toshiie|ja|前田利家|12=draft}}, an Important Cultural Property held by the {{ill|Maeda Ikutoku Association|ja|前田育徳会|12=draft}}); he speculates that its actual user was either {{ill|Hideyasu Kawajiri|ja|河尻秀隆|12=draft}}, who governed Kai after the fall of the Takeda clan, or a person in his circle.Ichirō Miura, ''Resurrecting the Takeda Army: Its Armor and Military Attire'', Miyabari Publishing, May 28, 2007, pp. 13–19. Furthermore, the chiseled section on its left shoulder is thought to be a possible sword wound scar from Hideyasu’s demise.}} * Paintings ** Colored Panel Painting of the Thirty-Six Immortal Poets – designated in [[1965]] (Showa 40) on August 19; donated jointly in [[1563]] (Eirōku 6) by Takeda Shingen and Takeda Yoshinobu, father and son ; Prefectural Designated Intangible Folk Cultural Properties * Miwa Shrine’s Taitei Kagura – one wooden plaque and one plate of the “Kagura Twenty-Five Order” – designated in [[1981]] ({{ill|Showa era|ja|昭和|12=draft}} 56) on March 12; said to have originated during the {{ill|Genroku period|ja|元禄|12=draft}} In addition, the Sakanai family—the shrine’s priesthood ({{ill|Shrine Priest|ja|神主|12=draft}})—has preserved documents spanning from the medieval period to modern times, which were transferred to the {{ill|Yamanashi Prefectural Museum|ja|山梨県立博物館|12=draft}} in Heisei 21. === "Tenshō Nenchū Ninomiya Festival Register" === Miwa Shrine has inherited the "Tenshō Nenchū Ninomiya Festival Register" (also known simply as the "Festival Register")Hirayama (1999), p.384. The register, consisting of 75 fascicles with subsequent lacunae, is noted for its extensive {{ill|Insect Damage|ja|虫損|12=draft}}. According to shrine tradition, it was compiled in [[1575]] (Tenshō 3), and among the names of Takeda retainers recorded therein, {{ill|Matsuki Awajimori|ja|末木家重|lt=Matsuki Awajimori|lt_ja=末木淡路守|12=draft}} (listed as “Ie-Chige”) is noted to have been active from the late Eirōku to the Tenshō period—retiring in Tenshō 9 and dying in Tenshō 15. Furthermore, both Amakawa Hyōbesuke and Amakawa Miyauchi-suke appear in the {{ill|Tenshō Jin-Go Petition|ja|天正壬午起請文|12=draft}}, which was submitted to the Tokugawa clan after the fall of the Takeda; this supports the shrine tradition that the register was compiled during the Tenshō period. == Miwa Shrine’s Taitei Kagura == During the spring festival, the {{ill|Taitei Kagura|ja|太々神楽|12=draft}} is performed in the shrine’s Kagura Hall within the precincts—during the evening ceremony and the following main festival—by members of the Miwa Shrine Kagura Preservation Society (all local parishioners). The repertoire includes a wide variety of dances, both maskless and masked, solo and small-group performances, with or without narrative elements. Among these are the Cleanse-the-Assembly Dance, Nation-Founding Dance, Four Pillars Dance, Descent Dance, Four Bows Dance, Group Dance, Sword Strike Dance, Preservation Deity Dance, National Orientation Dance, Fish Catching Dance, Sword Dance, Four Swords Dance, Treasure Ring Dance, Seed-Planting Dance, Great Serpent Dance, Evil-Illness Exorcism Dance, Fortune Change Dance, Ame-no-Iwato Dance, and Final Dance—a total of twenty surviving types. On the day of the festival, in the morning the {{ill|Urayasu Dance|ja|浦安の舞|12=draft}} is performed by young girls at the main shrine, after which the sacred spirit is transferred to the portable shrine which then departs toward Onoue. The Kagura continues until the portable shrine, having concluded its ritual at {{ill|Kinegami Shrine|ja|杵衡神社|12=draft}}, returns. According to the local tradition “On the Revival of This Kagura”, Miwa Shrine’s Kagura was revived when the main shrine building was reconstructed in [[1754]] (Hōreki 4) during the mid-Edo period. The “Kagura Twenty-Five Order” contained in the shrine documents is believed to date from the late Edo period, incorporating many elements of the old Ise-style order—including numerous maskless dances—which differ from the present repertoire. == References == {{Notes Help}} '''Notes''' {{Reflist|group="Notes"}} '''Sources''' {{Reflist}} == Bibliography == * {{ill|Makoto Horiuchi|ja|堀内眞|12=draft}}, “Yama”, in ''Yamanashi Prefecture History and Folklore'' (2003) – Volume 1, Chapter 4 * Makoto Horiuchi and Shigeru Takayama, “Faith”, in ''The Folklore of Ninomiya – Misaka Town, Higashiyatsushiro District –'' (Yamanashi Prefecture Historical and Folklore Survey Report, Volume 4, Heisei 9) == External Links == * [http://www.city.fuefuki.yamanashi.jp/kanko/shisetsu.php?id=83 Miwa Shrine – Fuefuki City] {{commonscat|Miwa-jinja, Fuefuki}} {{citation needed|Miwa Shrine, Fuefuki City}} {{shinto-stub}} {{pref-stub|pref=Yamanashi Prefecture}} {{citation needed|Miwa Shrine (Fuefuki City)}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Shrines in Yamanashi Prefecture]] [[Category:History of Fuefuki City]] [[Category:Buildings in Fuefuki City]] [[Category:National History Shrines]] [[Category:Former Prefectural Shrines in Yamanashi Prefecture]] [[Category:Kai Province]] [[Category:Ninomiya]] [[Category:Miwa Shrines]] [[Category:Important Cultural Properties in Fuefuki City]] [[Category:Designated Tangible Cultural Properties of Yamanashi Prefecture]] [[Category:Prefectural Designated Intangible Folk Cultural Properties]] [[Category:Mass Imported Shinto Cult Pages Needing Dummy Edit for Attribution and Review]] [[Category:11]] [[Category:New]] [[Category:remove from page of uncertain originality]][[Category:Completion tier 1]] [[Category:qq]][[sn:Miwa Shrine (Fuefuki)]][[Category:qq]] }} [[ja:美和神社 (笛吹市)]] [[sn:Miwa Shrine (Fuefuki City)]] [[ja:美和神社]] {{DEFAULTSORT:Miwa Shrine (Fuefuki City)}}

It is a [[Ninomiya (shrine)|Ninomiya]], or a second rank shrine in its province after the [[Ichinomiya]]. [[File:Miwa shrine Fuefuki-city.JPG|thumb|250px|Torii at Miwa Shrine (photo taken in April 2010)]] [[en:draft:Miwa Shrine (Fuefuki City)]] [[ja:美和神社 (笛吹市)]] [[ja:御袖天満宮]] [[sn:Miwa Shrine (Fuefuki City)]] [[File:Miwa shrine Fuefuki-city.JPG|thumb|250px|Miwa Shrine Torii (Photographed April 2010)]] '''Miwa Shrine''' (美和神社) is a {{ill|Shrine|ja|神社|12=draft}} located in {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|ja|山梨県|12=draft}} {{ill|Fuefuki City|ja|笛吹市|12=draft}}. It is a {{ill|Kokushi-Minaisha|ja|国史見在社|12=draft}}, and in {{ill|Kai Province|ja|甲斐国|12=draft}} it is known as {{ill|First Shrine|ja|一宮|lt=Second Shrine|lt_ja=二宮|12=draft}}, with its former shrine rank being {{ill|Prefectural Shrine|ja|県社|12=draft}}. == Deity == * {{ill|Ōmononushi|ja|大物主神|12=draft}} (Oomononushi-no-Kami) == Location == Miwa Shrine is situated in the eastern part of the {{ill|Kofu Basin|ja|甲府盆地|12=draft}} and enshrined in the Ninomiya district of the northwestern area. In ancient Kai Province, the early provincial capital ({{ill|Provincial Capital|ja|国府|12=draft}}) was located in {{ill|Kasuga Town, Fuefuki City|ja|笛吹市春日居町|12=draft}}, at the north-central edge of the basin, and is believed to have later been relocated to the vicinity of the national government office in {{ill|Misaka Town, Fuefuki City|ja|笛吹市御坂町|12=draft}}. The Misaka area is dotted with small to medium-sized burial mounds from the Kofun period—such as the {{ill|Kamekōdzuka Tumulus|ja|亀甲塚古墳|12=draft}} and {{ill|Baba Tumulus|ja|姥塚古墳|12=draft}}—as well as settlement ruins like the {{ill|Ninomiya Ruins|ja|二之宮遺跡|12=draft}}, and in ancient times, various governmental ruins and historic sites were spread throughout the area. According to “{{ill|Kōyō Gunkan|ja|甲陽軍鑑|12=draft}}”, in January of the preceding year [[1564]] (Eirōku 7) a retainer of Yoshinobu was punished for attempting a rebellion, and in the following year, [[1565]] (Eirōku 8), an incident occurred in which Yoshinobu himself was confined; however, from the records of the Zōritchō it is thought that the incident was uncovered in 1565 (Eirōku 8). Furthermore, in the following year [[1566]] (Eirōku 9), {{ill|Sanjō Consort|ja|三条夫人|12=draft}}—who was also the mother of Yoshinobu—offered armaments ({{ill|Armor|ja|具足|12=draft}}). On September 11, [[1573]] ({{ill|Genki era|ja|元亀|12=draft}} 4) immediately after the succession, {{ill|Takeda Katsuyori|ja|武田勝頼|12=draft}} ordered a prayer for enduring military fortune, and in [[1579]] ({{ill|Tenshō era|ja|天正|1=Tenshō (Momoyama period)|lt=Tenshō Era|12=draft}} 7) he imposed a prohibition. After the fall of the Takeda clan, in [[1582]] (Tenshō 10) prohibitions were issued by {{ill|Oda Nobunaga|ja|織田信長|12=draft}} and {{ill|Oda Nobutada|ja|織田信忠|12=draft}}, and in the following year [[1583]] (Tenshō 11) the shrine received a guarantee for its estates from {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|ja|徳川家康|12=draft}}, with the estates finally confirmed in [[1589]] (Tenshō 17) by a land survey conducted by {{ill|Inatadashi|ja|伊奈忠次|12=draft}}. During the era of Toyotomi-affiliated daimyō, the shrine received donations of estates from {{ill|Kato Mitsuyasu|ja|加藤光泰|12=draft}} and the {{ill|Asano clan|ja|浅野氏|12=draft}}. As a ritual, from the Sengoku period through early modern times a joint pilgrimage—known as the “Three-Shrine Onmiyuki”—was mandated. This ritual, performed at the Shingen Embankment ({{ill|Shingen Embankment|ja|信玄堤|12=draft}}) in {{ill|Kai City|ja|甲斐市|12=draft}}, involved the three shrines of Ichinomiya and Sannomiya; the summer onmiyuki was held on the third Ino day in April, and the winter onmiyuki on the second Ino day in November. During the Meiji period, with the prohibition of the three-shrine pilgrimage, the Yamamiya Onmiyuki (the Ninomiya Onmiyuki), which had been held on the first day of March, was rescheduled to April 15 and designated as the spring festival; although this event was interrupted for a time in the postwar era, it is now held on the first Sunday of April with the Taitei Kagura offered in dedication. Also, every February 8 the {{ill|Yudate Ritual|ja|湯立神事|12=draft}} is observed. Miwa Shrine’s Yudate Ritual, which is accompanied by the prayer dance of Sarutahiko, is the only surviving Yudate Ritual in the prefecture. According to a locally handed‐down document from 1826 (Bunsei 9), the Ninomiya Yudate was held separately on February 8—distinct from the Taitei Kagura held in mid‐March—and the dance of Sarutahiko is also recorded in {{ill|Uramihankuwa|ja|裏見寒話|12=draft}}. The shrine priesthood is provided by the Sakanai family, and {{ill|Sakanai Sōō|ja|坂名井聡翁|12=draft}} is known as a Kokugaku scholar. == Cultural Properties, etc. == [[File:Miwa-shrine Yutateshinji Kagura.JPG|thumb|250px|Prayer Dance of Sarutahiko during the Yudate Ritual (Photographed February 8, 2011)]] [[File:Miwa-shrine Yutateshinji A.JPG|thumb|250px|Ritual during the Yudate Ritual (Photographed February 8, 2011)]] [[File:Miwa-shrine Yutateshinji B.JPG|thumb|250px|Soaking bamboo leaves in boiling water and pouring it on worshippers (Photographed February 8, 2011)]] ; Important Cultural Properties (National Designation) * Sculpture ** Wooden Standing Statue of Ōmononushi – designated in [[1906]] (Meiji 39) on September 6; a work from the Heian period{{National Designated Cultural Properties Database|201|2937|Wooden Standing Statue of Ōmononushi}} (accessed May 19, 2017){{PDFlink|[https://www.city.fuefuki.yamanashi.jp/documents/607/5bf21d9faea4d.pdf Fuefuki City Cultural Properties Guidebook]}} – Fuefuki City, accessed December 23, 2019. ; Designated Tangible Cultural Properties of Yamanashi Prefecture * Crafts ** White Thread-Tied Armor (fragmentary) – designated in [[1986]] (Showa 61) on March 19; a work from the Nanboku-chō period{{Refnest|group="Notes"|Armor researcher Ichirō Miura has estimated, based on its manufacturing technique, that this armor dates from the period of {{ill|Takeda Nobunari|ja|武田信成|12=draft}} and {{ill|Takeda Nobuharu|ja|武田信春|lt=Nobuharu|lt_ja=信春|12=draft}}.Ichirō Miura, ''Resurrecting the Takeda Army: Its Armor and Military Attire'', Miyabari Publishing, May 28, 2007, pp. 7–13}} ** Vermilion Talisman and Red Thread Unarmored Armor with Accompanying Targe – designated in 1986 (Showa 61) on March 19; a legendary coming-of-age armor of {{ill|Takeda Shingen|ja|武田信玄|lt=Takeda Harunobu|lt_ja=武田晴信|12=draft}}{{Refnest|group="Notes"|However, Ichirō Miura notes that from its style this armor is a work of the Tenshō period—later than the time of Shingen’s coming-of-age—and that its manufacturing technique and design share commonalities with the armors of military commanders active under the Oda–Toyotomi regime (such as the gold small-talisman white thread unarmored armor of {{ill|Maeda Toshiie|ja|前田利家|12=draft}}, an Important Cultural Property held by the {{ill|Maeda Ikutoku Association|ja|前田育徳会|12=draft}}); he speculates that its actual user was either {{ill|Hideyasu Kawajiri|ja|河尻秀隆|12=draft}}, who governed Kai after the fall of the Takeda clan, or a person in his circle.Ichirō Miura, ''Resurrecting the Takeda Army: Its Armor and Military Attire'', Miyabari Publishing, May 28, 2007, pp. 13–19. Furthermore, the chiseled section on its left shoulder is thought to be a possible sword wound scar from Hideyasu’s demise.}} * Paintings ** Colored Panel Painting of the Thirty-Six Immortal Poets – designated in [[1965]] (Showa 40) on August 19; donated jointly in [[1563]] (Eirōku 6) by Takeda Shingen and Takeda Yoshinobu, father and son ; Prefectural Designated Intangible Folk Cultural Properties * Miwa Shrine’s Taitei Kagura – one wooden plaque and one plate of the “Kagura Twenty-Five Order” – designated in [[1981]] ({{ill|Showa era|ja|昭和|12=draft}} 56) on March 12; said to have originated during the {{ill|Genroku period|ja|元禄|12=draft}} In addition, the Sakanai family—the shrine’s priesthood ({{ill|Shrine Priest|ja|神主|12=draft}})—has preserved documents spanning from the medieval period to modern times, which were transferred to the {{ill|Yamanashi Prefectural Museum|ja|山梨県立博物館|12=draft}} in Heisei 21. === "Tenshō Nenchū Ninomiya Festival Register" === Miwa Shrine has inherited the "Tenshō Nenchū Ninomiya Festival Register" (also known simply as the "Festival Register")Hirayama (1999), p.384. The register, consisting of 75 fascicles with subsequent lacunae, is noted for its extensive {{ill|Insect Damage|ja|虫損|12=draft}}. According to shrine tradition, it was compiled in [[1575]] (Tenshō 3), and among the names of Takeda retainers recorded therein, {{ill|Matsuki Awajimori|ja|末木家重|lt=Matsuki Awajimori|lt_ja=末木淡路守|12=draft}} (listed as “Ie-Chige”) is noted to have been active from the late Eirōku to the Tenshō period—retiring in Tenshō 9 and dying in Tenshō 15. Furthermore, both Amakawa Hyōbesuke and Amakawa Miyauchi-suke appear in the {{ill|Tenshō Jin-Go Petition|ja|天正壬午起請文|12=draft}}, which was submitted to the Tokugawa clan after the fall of the Takeda; this supports the shrine tradition that the register was compiled during the Tenshō period. == Miwa Shrine’s Taitei Kagura == During the spring festival, the {{ill|Taitei Kagura|ja|太々神楽|12=draft}} is performed in the shrine’s Kagura Hall within the precincts—during the evening ceremony and the following main festival—by members of the Miwa Shrine Kagura Preservation Society (all local parishioners). The repertoire includes a wide variety of dances, both maskless and masked, solo and small-group performances, with or without narrative elements. Among these are the Cleanse-the-Assembly Dance, Nation-Founding Dance, Four Pillars Dance, Descent Dance, Four Bows Dance, Group Dance, Sword Strike Dance, Preservation Deity Dance, National Orientation Dance, Fish Catching Dance, Sword Dance, Four Swords Dance, Treasure Ring Dance, Seed-Planting Dance, Great Serpent Dance, Evil-Illness Exorcism Dance, Fortune Change Dance, Ame-no-Iwato Dance, and Final Dance—a total of twenty surviving types. On the day of the festival, in the morning the {{ill|Urayasu Dance|ja|浦安の舞|12=draft}} is performed by young girls at the main shrine, after which the sacred spirit is transferred to the portable shrine which then departs toward Onoue. The Kagura continues until the portable shrine, having concluded its ritual at {{ill|Kinegami Shrine|ja|杵衡神社|12=draft}}, returns. According to the local tradition “On the Revival of This Kagura”, Miwa Shrine’s Kagura was revived when the main shrine building was reconstructed in [[1754]] (Hōreki 4) during the mid-Edo period. The “Kagura Twenty-Five Order” contained in the shrine documents is believed to date from the late Edo period, incorporating many elements of the old Ise-style order—including numerous maskless dances—which differ from the present repertoire. == See Also == *{{ill|Seichi junrei|ja|巡礼 (通俗)|12=draft}} * {{ill|Ōyamadera|ja|大山寺 (尾道市)|12=draft}} == References == {{reflist}} == Bibliography == * ''Hiroshima Encyclopedia'' (広島県大百科事典〈下巻〉). [[File:Miwa shrine Fuefuki-city.JPG|thumb|250px|Torii at Miwa Shrine (photo taken in April 2010)]] [[en:draft:Miwa Shrine (Fuefuki City)]] [[ja:美和神社 (笛吹市)]] [[ja:御袖天満宮]] [[sn:Miwa Shrine (Fuefuki City)]] [[File:Miwa shrine Fuefuki-city.JPG|thumb|250px|Miwa Shrine Torii (Photographed April 2010)]] '''Miwa Shrine''' (美和神社) is a {{ill|Shrine|ja|神社|12=draft}} located in {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|ja|山梨県|12=draft}} {{ill|Fuefuki City|ja|笛吹市|12=draft}}. It is a {{ill|Kokushi-Minaisha|ja|国史見在社|12=draft}}, and in {{ill|Kai Province|ja|甲斐国|12=draft}} it is known as {{ill|First Shrine|ja|一宮|lt=Second Shrine|lt_ja=二宮|12=draft}}, with its former shrine rank being {{ill|Prefectural Shrine|ja|県社|12=draft}}. == Deity == * {{ill|Ōmononushi|ja|大物主神|12=draft}} (Oomononushi-no-Kami) == Location == Miwa Shrine is situated in the eastern part of the {{ill|Kofu Basin|ja|甲府盆地|12=draft}} and enshrined in the Ninomiya district of the northwestern area. In ancient Kai Province, the early provincial capital ({{ill|Provincial Capital|ja|国府|12=draft}}) was located in {{ill|Kasuga Town, Fuefuki City|ja|笛吹市春日居町|12=draft}}, at the north-central edge of the basin, and is believed to have later been relocated to the vicinity of the national government office in {{ill|Misaka Town, Fuefuki City|ja|笛吹市御坂町|12=draft}}. The Misaka area is dotted with small to medium-sized burial mounds from the Kofun period—such as the {{ill|Kamekōdzuka Tumulus|ja|亀甲塚古墳|12=draft}} and {{ill|Baba Tumulus|ja|姥塚古墳|12=draft}}—as well as settlement ruins like the {{ill|Ninomiya Ruins|ja|二之宮遺跡|12=draft}}, and in ancient times, various governmental ruins and historic sites were spread throughout the area. Under the Ritsuryō system, the area was equated with Inoue Village in Yamanashi District, and the name “Ninomiya” is derived from its proximity to the national administrative office and Miwa Shrine. In the early modern period, Ninomiya Village was established, centered around Miwa Shrine. The shrine, located in the Ninomiya district, is designated as {{ill|Satomiya|ja|里宮|12=draft}}, while in the Oyama area to the east of Ninomiya stands {{ill|Yamamiya|ja|山宮|12=draft}} in the form of {{ill|Kinegami Shrine|ja|杵衡神社|12=draft}}. == History == It is generally believed that Miwa Shrine was enshrined by being invited from {{ill|Ōmiya Shrine|ja|大神神社|12=draft}} of {{ill|Yamato Province|ja|Yamato Province|12=draft}} ({{ill|Nara Prefecture|ja|奈良県|12=draft}}), which regards {{ill|Mount Miwa|ja|三輪山|12=draft}} as its shintai, and that after being transferred to the {{ill|Kinegami Shrine|ja|杵衡神社|12=draft}} in Onoe Village, it was newly relocated to Ninomiya. According to the texts “{{ill|Kai Kokashiki-ji|ja|甲斐国社記・寺記|12=draft}}” and “{{ill|Kai Kokushi|ja|甲斐国志|12=draft}}”, the shrine’s origins are said to date back to the time of {{ill|Emperor Keikō|ja|景行天皇|12=draft}}, when the provincial governor of Kai ({{ill|Provincial Governor of Kai|ja|甲斐国造|12=draft}}) and {{ill|Shio-umi Ashin|ja|塩海足尼|12=draft}} performed the enshrinement. The earliest historical record appears in an entry of “{{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|ja|日本三代実録|12=draft}}” dated June 8, [[863]] ({{ill|Jōgan era|ja|Jōgan|12=draft}} 5), which states that on that day Miwa Shrine was conferred the junior fifth rank and granted the title “Ninomiya” by {{ill|Emperor Ichijō|ja|一条天皇|12=draft}}. In the medieval period, it received veneration from the {{ill|Takeda clan|ja|武田氏|12=draft}}—the guardians of Kai—and in [[1479]] ({{ill|Bunmei era|ja|Bunmei|12=draft}} 11) the lord of {{ill|Shinano Province|ja|信濃国|12=draft}}’s {{ill|Saku District|ja|佐久郡|12=draft}}, the {{ill|Ōi clan|ja|大井氏|12=draft}}, invaded Kai; during this time Miwa Shrine also suffered from warfare. In the period of {{ill|Takeda Shigetora|ja|武田信虎|12=draft}}, the shrine was granted estates in {{ill|Manriki Village|ja|万力郷|12=draft}} in {{ill|Yamanashi District|ja|山梨郡|12=draft}} (present-day {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|ja|山梨県|12=draft}}), and in [[1557]] ({{ill|Kōji era|ja|Kōji (Muromachi period)|lt=Kōji|lt_ja=Kōji|12=draft}} 3) it received a charter from {{ill|Takeda Shingen|ja|武田信玄|lt=Takeda Harunobu|lt_ja=武田晴信|12=draft}} (Shingen), alongside {{ill|Asama Shrine (Fuefuki City)|ja|浅間神社 (笛吹市)|lt=Asama Shrine|lt_ja=浅間神社|12=draft}} (located in Ichinomiya, Ichinomiya Town, Fuefuki City), {{ill|Tamamoro Shrine|ja|玉諸神社|lt=Tamamoro Shrine|lt_ja=玉諸神社|12=draft}} in Kōfu City, and the Takeda clan’s tutelary shrine, {{ill|Takeda Hachiman Shrine|ja|武田八幡宮|12=draft}} (in {{ill|Nirasaki City|ja|韮崎市|12=draft}}), among others—exempting them from serving at Fuchū Hachiman Shrine (currently {{ill|Hachiman Shrine (Kōfu)|ja|八幡神社 (甲府市宮前町)|12=draft}} in Kōfu City). Also, every February 8 the {{ill|Yudate Ritual|ja|湯立神事|12=draft}} is observed. Miwa Shrine’s Yudate Ritual, which is accompanied by the prayer dance of Sarutahiko, is the only surviving Yudate Ritual in the prefecture. According to a locally handed‐down document from 1826 (Bunsei 9), the Ninomiya Yudate was held separately on February 8—distinct from the Taitei Kagura held in mid‐March—and the dance of Sarutahiko is also recorded in {{ill|Uramihankuwa|ja|裏見寒話|12=draft}}. The shrine priesthood is provided by the Sakanai family, and {{ill|Sakanai Sōō|ja|坂名井聡翁|12=draft}} is known as a Kokugaku scholar. == Cultural Properties, etc. == [[File:Miwa-shrine Yutateshinji Kagura.JPG|thumb|250px|Prayer Dance of Sarutahiko during the Yudate Ritual (Photographed February 8, 2011)]] [[File:Miwa-shrine Yutateshinji A.JPG|thumb|250px|Ritual during the Yudate Ritual (Photographed February 8, 2011)]] [[File:Miwa-shrine Yutateshinji B.JPG|thumb|250px|Soaking bamboo leaves in boiling water and pouring it on worshippers (Photographed February 8, 2011)]] ; Important Cultural Properties (National Designation) * Sculpture ** Wooden Standing Statue of Ōmononushi – designated in [[1906]] (Meiji 39) on September 6; a work from the Heian period{{National Designated Cultural Properties Database|201|2937|Wooden Standing Statue of Ōmononushi}} (accessed May 19, 2017){{PDFlink|[https://www.city.fuefuki.yamanashi.jp/documents/607/5bf21d9faea4d.pdf Fuefuki City Cultural Properties Guidebook]}} – Fuefuki City, accessed December 23, 2019. ; Designated Tangible Cultural Properties of Yamanashi Prefecture * Crafts ** White Thread-Tied Armor (fragmentary) – designated in [[1986]] (Showa 61) on March 19; a work from the Nanboku-chō period{{Refnest|group="Notes"|Armor researcher Ichirō Miura has estimated, based on its manufacturing technique, that this armor dates from the period of {{ill|Takeda Nobunari|ja|武田信成|12=draft}} and {{ill|Takeda Nobuharu|ja|武田信春|lt=Nobuharu|lt_ja=信春|12=draft}}.Ichirō Miura, ''Resurrecting the Takeda Army: Its Armor and Military Attire'', Miyabari Publishing, May 28, 2007, pp. 7–13}} ** Vermilion Talisman and Red Thread Unarmored Armor with Accompanying Targe – designated in 1986 (Showa 61) on March 19; a legendary coming-of-age armor of {{ill|Takeda Shingen|ja|武田信玄|lt=Takeda Harunobu|lt_ja=武田晴信|12=draft}}{{Refnest|group="Notes"|However, Ichirō Miura notes that from its style this armor is a work of the Tenshō period—later than the time of Shingen’s coming-of-age—and that its manufacturing technique and design share commonalities with the armors of military commanders active under the Oda–Toyotomi regime (such as the gold small-talisman white thread unarmored armor of {{ill|Maeda Toshiie|ja|前田利家|12=draft}}, an Important Cultural Property held by the {{ill|Maeda Ikutoku Association|ja|前田育徳会|12=draft}}); he speculates that its actual user was either {{ill|Hideyasu Kawajiri|ja|河尻秀隆|12=draft}}, who governed Kai after the fall of the Takeda clan, or a person in his circle.Ichirō Miura, ''Resurrecting the Takeda Army: Its Armor and Military Attire'', Miyabari Publishing, May 28, 2007, pp. 13–19. Furthermore, the chiseled section on its left shoulder is thought to be a possible sword wound scar from Hideyasu’s demise.}} * Paintings ** Colored Panel Painting of the Thirty-Six Immortal Poets – designated in [[1965]] (Showa 40) on August 19; donated jointly in [[1563]] (Eirōku 6) by Takeda Shingen and Takeda Yoshinobu, father and son ; Prefectural Designated Intangible Folk Cultural Properties * Miwa Shrine’s Taitei Kagura – one wooden plaque and one plate of the “Kagura Twenty-Five Order” – designated in [[1981]] ({{ill|Showa era|ja|昭和|12=draft}} 56) on March 12; said to have originated during the {{ill|Genroku period|ja|元禄|12=draft}} In addition, the Sakanai family—the shrine’s priesthood ({{ill|Shrine Priest|ja|神主|12=draft}})—has preserved documents spanning from the medieval period to modern times, which were transferred to the {{ill|Yamanashi Prefectural Museum|ja|山梨県立博物館|12=draft}} in Heisei 21. === "Tenshō Nenchū Ninomiya Festival Register" === Miwa Shrine has inherited the "Tenshō Nenchū Ninomiya Festival Register" (also known simply as the "Festival Register")Hirayama (1999), p.384. The register, consisting of 75 fascicles with subsequent lacunae, is noted for its extensive {{ill|Insect Damage|ja|虫損|12=draft}}. According to shrine tradition, it was compiled in [[1575]] (Tenshō 3), and among the names of Takeda retainers recorded therein, {{ill|Matsuki Awajimori|ja|末木家重|lt=Matsuki Awajimori|lt_ja=末木淡路守|12=draft}} (listed as “Ie-Chige”) is noted to have been active from the late Eirōku to the Tenshō period—retiring in Tenshō 9 and dying in Tenshō 15. Furthermore, both Amakawa Hyōbesuke and Amakawa Miyauchi-suke appear in the {{ill|Tenshō Jin-Go Petition|ja|天正壬午起請文|12=draft}}, which was submitted to the Tokugawa clan after the fall of the Takeda; this supports the shrine tradition that the register was compiled during the Tenshō period. == Miwa Shrine’s Taitei Kagura == During the spring festival, the {{ill|Taitei Kagura|ja|太々神楽|12=draft}} is performed in the shrine’s Kagura Hall within the precincts—during the evening ceremony and the following main festival—by members of the Miwa Shrine Kagura Preservation Society (all local parishioners). The repertoire includes a wide variety of dances, both maskless and masked, solo and small-group performances, with or without narrative elements. Among these are the Cleanse-the-Assembly Dance, Nation-Founding Dance, Four Pillars Dance, Descent Dance, Four Bows Dance, Group Dance, Sword Strike Dance, Preservation Deity Dance, National Orientation Dance, Fish Catching Dance, Sword Dance, Four Swords Dance, Treasure Ring Dance, Seed-Planting Dance, Great Serpent Dance, Evil-Illness Exorcism Dance, Fortune Change Dance, Ame-no-Iwato Dance, and Final Dance—a total of twenty surviving types. On the day of the festival, in the morning the {{ill|Urayasu Dance|ja|浦安の舞|12=draft}} is performed by young girls at the main shrine, after which the sacred spirit is transferred to the portable shrine which then departs toward Onoue. The Kagura continues until the portable shrine, having concluded its ritual at {{ill|Kinegami Shrine|ja|杵衡神社|12=draft}}, returns. According to the local tradition “On the Revival of This Kagura”, Miwa Shrine’s Kagura was revived when the main shrine building was reconstructed in [[1754]] (Hōreki 4) during the mid-Edo period. The “Kagura Twenty-Five Order” contained in the shrine documents is believed to date from the late Edo period, incorporating many elements of the old Ise-style order—including numerous maskless dances—which differ from the present repertoire. == See Also == *{{ill|Seichi junrei|ja|巡礼 (通俗)|12=draft}} * {{ill|Ōyamadera|ja|大山寺 (尾道市)|12=draft}} == References == {{reflist}} == Bibliography == * ''Hiroshima Encyclopedia'' (広島県大百科事典〈下巻〉). Chūgoku Shimbun, 1982. == External Links == * [http://misodetenmangu.or.jp/ Official website of Misode Tenmangū] {{Shinto pilgrimage}} {{Shinto-stub}} {{commonscat|Miwa-jinja, Fuefuki}} {{citation Former {{ill|Prefectural Shrine|ja|県社|12=draft}} |foundation = (trad.) Period of {{ill|Emperor Keikō|ja|景行天皇|12=draft}} |main_shrine = {{ill|Nagare-zukuri|ja|流造|12=draft}} |alternative_names = |subsidiary = |festival = {{ill|March 15|ja|3月15日|12=draft}} |ritual = Yudate Ritual (February 8) |map = {{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=13|frame-align=center|frame-width=200}} }} {{ill|Miwa Shrine (Fuefuki City)|ja|美和神社 (笛吹市)|lt=Miwa Shrine|12=draft}} (美和神社) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in [[Japan]]. It is a [[Ninomiya (shrine)|Ninomiya]], or a second rank shrine in its province after the [[Ichinomiya]]. [[File:Miwa shrine Fuefuki-city.JPG|thumb|250px|Torii at Miwa Shrine (photo taken in April 2010)]] [[en:draft:Miwa Shrine (Fuefuki City)]] [[ja:美和神社 (笛吹市)]] [[ja:御袖天満宮]] [[sn:Miwa Shrine (Fuefuki City)]] [[File:Miwa shrine Fuefuki-city.JPG|thumb|250px|Miwa Shrine Torii (Photographed April 2010)]] '''Miwa Shrine''' (美和神社) is a {{ill|Shrine|ja|神社|12=draft}} located in {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|ja|山梨県|12=draft}} {{ill|Fuefuki City|ja|笛吹市|12=draft}}. It is a {{ill|Kokushi-Minaisha|ja|国史見在社|12=draft}}, and in {{ill|Kai Province|ja|甲斐国|12=draft}} it is known as {{ill|First Shrine|ja|一宮|lt=Second Shrine|lt_ja=二宮|12=draft}}, with its former shrine rank being {{ill|Prefectural Shrine|ja|県社|12=draft}}. == Deity == * {{ill|Ōmononushi|ja|大物主神|12=draft}} (Oomononushi-no-Kami) == Location == Miwa Shrine is situated in the eastern part of the {{ill|Kofu Basin|ja|甲府盆地|12=draft}} and enshrined in the Ninomiya district of the northwestern area. In ancient Kai Province, the early provincial capital ({{ill|Provincial Capital|ja|国府|12=draft}}) was located in {{ill|Kasuga Town, Fuefuki City|ja|笛吹市春日居町|12=draft}}, at the north-central edge of the basin, and is believed to have later been relocated to the vicinity of the national government office in {{ill|Misaka Town, Fuefuki City|ja|笛吹市御坂町|12=draft}}. The Misaka area is dotted with small to medium-sized burial mounds from the Kofun period—such as the {{ill|Kamekōdzuka Tumulus|ja|亀甲塚古墳|12=draft}} and {{ill|Baba Tumulus|ja|姥塚古墳|12=draft}}—as well as settlement ruins like the {{ill|Ninomiya Ruins|ja|二之宮遺跡|12=draft}}, and in ancient times, various governmental ruins and historic sites were spread throughout the area. Under the Ritsuryō system, the area was equated with Inoue Village in Yamanashi District, and the name “Ninomiya” is derived from its proximity to the national administrative office and Miwa Shrine. In the early modern period, Ninomiya Village was established, centered around Miwa Shrine. The shrine, located in the Ninomiya district, is designated as {{ill|Satomiya|ja|里宮|12=draft}}, while in the Oyama area to the east of Ninomiya stands {{ill|Yamamiya|ja|山宮|12=draft}} in the form of {{ill|Kinegami Shrine|ja|杵衡神社|12=draft}}. == History == It is generally believed that Miwa Shrine was enshrined by being invited from {{ill|Ōmiya Shrine|ja|大神神社|12=draft}} of {{ill|Yamato Province|ja|Yamato Province|12=draft}} ({{ill|Nara Prefecture|ja|奈良県|12=draft}}), which regards {{ill|Mount Miwa|ja|三輪山|12=draft}} as its shintai, and that after being transferred to the {{ill|Kinegami Shrine|ja|杵衡神社|12=draft}} in Onoe Village, it was newly relocated to Ninomiya. According to the texts “{{ill|Kai Kokashiki-ji|ja|甲斐国社記・寺記|12=draft}}” and “{{ill|Kai Kokushi|ja|甲斐国志|12=draft}}”, the shrine’s origins are said to date back to the time of {{ill|Emperor Keikō|ja|景行天皇|12=draft}}, when the provincial governor of Kai ({{ill|Provincial Governor of Kai|ja|甲斐国造|12=draft}}) and {{ill|Shio-umi Ashin|ja|塩海足尼|12=draft}} performed the enshrinement. The earliest historical record appears in an entry of “{{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|ja|日本三代実録|12=draft}}” dated June 8, [[863]] ({{ill|Jōgan era|ja|Jōgan|12=draft}} 5), which states that on that day Miwa Shrine was conferred the junior fifth rank and granted the title “Ninomiya” by {{ill|Emperor Ichijō|ja|一条天皇|12=draft}}. In the medieval period, it received veneration from the {{ill|Takeda clan|ja|武田氏|12=draft}}—the guardians of Kai—and in [[1479]] ({{ill|Bunmei era|ja|Bunmei|12=draft}} 11) the lord of {{ill|Shinano Province|ja|信濃国|12=draft}}’s {{ill|Saku District|ja|佐久郡|12=draft}}, the {{ill|Ōi clan|ja|大井氏|12=draft}}, invaded Kai; during this time Miwa Shrine also suffered from warfare. In the period of {{ill|Takeda Shigetora|ja|武田信虎|12=draft}}, the shrine was granted estates in {{ill|Manriki Village|ja|万力郷|12=draft}} in {{ill|Yamanashi District|ja|山梨郡|12=draft}} (present-day {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|ja|山梨県|12=draft}}), and in [[1557]] ({{ill|Kōji era|ja|Kōji (Muromachi period)|lt=Kōji|lt_ja=Kōji|12=draft}} 3) it received a charter from {{ill|Takeda Shingen|ja|武田信玄|lt=Takeda Harunobu|lt_ja=武田晴信|12=draft}} (Shingen), alongside {{ill|Asama Shrine (Fuefuki City)|ja|浅間神社 (笛吹市)|lt=Asama Shrine|lt_ja=浅間神社|12=draft}} (located in Ichinomiya, Ichinomiya Town, Fuefuki City), {{ill|Tamamoro Shrine|ja|玉諸神社|lt=Tamamoro Shrine|lt_ja=玉諸神社|12=draft}} in Kōfu City, and the Takeda clan’s tutelary shrine, {{ill|Takeda Hachiman Shrine|ja|武田八幡宮|12=draft}} (in {{ill|Nirasaki City|ja|韮崎市|12=draft}}), among others—exempting them from serving at Fuchū Hachiman Shrine (currently {{ill|Hachiman Shrine (Kōfu)|ja|八幡神社 (甲府市宮前町)|12=draft}} in Kōfu City). In June [[1565]] (Eiroku 8) a {{ill|Tachi (sword)|ja|太刀|12=draft}} offering was made by a retainer of {{ill|Takeda Yoshinobu|ja|武田義信|12=draft}}, the heir of the Takeda family, as recorded in the Miwa Shrine document “Kōshū Ninomiya Zōritchō”. According to “{{ill|Kōyō Gunkan|ja|甲陽軍鑑|12=draft}}”, in January of the preceding year [[1564]] (Eirōku 7) a retainer of Yoshinobu was punished for attempting a rebellion, and in the following year, [[1565]] (Eirōku 8), an incident occurred in which Yoshinobu himself was confined; however, from the records of the Zōritchō it is thought that the incident was uncovered in 1565 (Eirōku 8). Furthermore, in the following year [[1566]] (Eirōku 9), {{ill|Sanjō Consort|ja|三条夫人|12=draft}}—who was also the mother of Yoshinobu—offered armaments ({{ill|Armor|ja|具足|12=draft}}). On September 11, [[1573]] ({{ill|Genki era|ja|元亀|12=draft}} 4) immediately after the succession, {{ill|Takeda Katsuyori|ja|武田勝頼|12=draft}} ordered a prayer for enduring military fortune, and in [[1579]] ({{ill|Tenshō era|ja|天正|1=Tenshō (Momoyama period)|lt=Tenshō Era|12=draft}} 7) he imposed a prohibition. After the fall of the Takeda clan, in [[1582]] (Tenshō 10) prohibitions were issued by {{ill|Oda Nobunaga|ja|織田信長|12=draft}} and {{ill|Oda Nobutada|ja|織田信忠|12=draft}}, and in the following year [[1583]] (Tenshō 11) the shrine received a guarantee for its estates from {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|ja|徳川家康|12=draft}}, with the estates finally confirmed in [[1589]] (Tenshō 17) by a land survey conducted by {{ill|Inatadashi|ja|伊奈忠次|12=draft}}. During the era of Toyotomi-affiliated daimyō, the shrine received donations of estates from {{ill|Kato Mitsuyasu|ja|加藤光泰|12=draft}} and the {{ill|Asano clan|ja|浅野氏|12=draft}}. As a ritual, from the Sengoku period through early modern times a joint pilgrimage—known as the “Three-Shrine Onmiyuki”—was mandated. This ritual, performed at the Shingen Embankment ({{ill|Shingen Embankment|ja|信玄堤|12=draft}}) in {{ill|Kai City|ja|甲斐市|12=draft}}, involved the three shrines of Ichinomiya and Sannomiya; the summer onmiyuki was held on the third Ino day in April, and the winter onmiyuki on the second Ino day in November. During the Meiji period, with the prohibition of the three-shrine pilgrimage, the Yamamiya Onmiyuki (the Ninomiya Onmiyuki), which had been held on the first day of March, was rescheduled to April 15 and designated as the spring festival; although this event was interrupted for a time in the postwar era, it is now held on the first Sunday of April with the Taitei Kagura offered in dedication. Also, every February 8 the {{ill|Yudate Ritual|ja|湯立神事|12=draft}} is observed. Miwa Shrine’s Yudate Ritual, which is accompanied by the prayer dance of Sarutahiko, is the only surviving Yudate Ritual in the prefecture. According to a locally handed‐down document from 1826 (Bunsei 9), the Ninomiya Yudate was held separately on February 8—distinct from the Taitei Kagura held in mid‐March—and the dance of Sarutahiko is also recorded in {{ill|Uramihankuwa|ja|裏見寒話|12=draft}}. The shrine priesthood is provided by the Sakanai family, and {{ill|Sakanai Sōō|ja|坂名井聡翁|12=draft}} is known as a Kokugaku scholar. == Cultural Properties, etc. == [[File:Miwa-shrine Yutateshinji Kagura.JPG|thumb|250px|Prayer Dance of Sarutahiko during the Yudate Ritual (Photographed February 8, 2011)]] [[File:Miwa-shrine Yutateshinji A.JPG|thumb|250px|Ritual during the Yudate Ritual (Photographed February 8, 2011)]] [[File:Miwa-shrine Yutateshinji B.JPG|thumb|250px|Soaking bamboo leaves in boiling water and pouring it on worshippers (Photographed February 8, 2011)]] ; Important Cultural Properties (National Designation) * Sculpture ** Wooden Standing Statue of Ōmononushi – designated in [[1906]] (Meiji 39) on September 6; a work from the Heian period{{National Designated Cultural Properties Database|201|2937|Wooden Standing Statue of Ōmononushi}} (accessed May 19, 2017){{PDFlink|[https://www.city.fuefuki.yamanashi.jp/documents/607/5bf21d9faea4d.pdf Fuefuki City Cultural Properties Guidebook]}} – Fuefuki City, accessed December 23, 2019. ; Designated Tangible Cultural Properties of Yamanashi Prefecture * Crafts ** White Thread-Tied Armor (fragmentary) – designated in [[1986]] (Showa 61) on March 19; a work from the Nanboku-chō period{{Refnest|group="Notes"|Armor researcher Ichirō Miura has estimated, based on its manufacturing technique, that this armor dates from the period of {{ill|Takeda Nobunari|ja|武田信成|12=draft}} and {{ill|Takeda Nobuharu|ja|武田信春|lt=Nobuharu|lt_ja=信春|12=draft}}.Ichirō Miura, ''Resurrecting the Takeda Army: Its Armor and Military Attire'', Miyabari Publishing, May 28, 2007, pp. 7–13}} ** Vermilion Talisman and Red Thread Unarmored Armor with Accompanying Targe – designated in 1986 (Showa 61) on March 19; a legendary coming-of-age armor of {{ill|Takeda Shingen|ja|武田信玄|lt=Takeda Harunobu|lt_ja=武田晴信|12=draft}}{{Refnest|group="Notes"|However, Ichirō Miura notes that from its style this armor is a work of the Tenshō period—later than the time of Shingen’s coming-of-age—and that its manufacturing technique and design share commonalities with the armors of military commanders active under the Oda–Toyotomi regime (such as the gold small-talisman white thread unarmored armor of {{ill|Maeda Toshiie|ja|前田利家|12=draft}}, an Important Cultural Property held by the {{ill|Maeda Ikutoku Association|ja|前田育徳会|12=draft}}); he speculates that its actual user was either {{ill|Hideyasu Kawajiri|ja|河尻秀隆|12=draft}}, who governed Kai after the fall of the Takeda clan, or a person in his circle.Ichirō Miura, ''Resurrecting the Takeda Army: Its Armor and Military Attire'', Miyabari Publishing, May 28, 2007, pp. 13–19. Furthermore, the chiseled section on its left shoulder is thought to be a possible sword wound scar from Hideyasu’s demise.}} * Paintings ** Colored Panel Painting of the Thirty-Six Immortal Poets – designated in [[1965]] (Showa 40) on August 19; donated jointly in [[1563]] (Eirōku 6) by Takeda Shingen and Takeda Yoshinobu, father and son ; Prefectural Designated Intangible Folk Cultural Properties * Miwa Shrine’s Taitei Kagura – one wooden plaque and one plate of the “Kagura Twenty-Five Order” – designated in [[1981]] ({{ill|Showa era|ja|昭和|12=draft}} 56) on March 12; said to have originated during the {{ill|Genroku period|ja|元禄|12=draft}} In addition, the Sakanai family—the shrine’s priesthood ({{ill|Shrine Priest|ja|神主|12=draft}})—has preserved documents spanning from the medieval period to modern times, which were transferred to the {{ill|Yamanashi Prefectural Museum|ja|山梨県立博物館|12=draft}} in Heisei 21. === "Tenshō Nenchū Ninomiya Festival Register" === Miwa Shrine has inherited the "Tenshō Nenchū Ninomiya Festival Register" (also known simply as the "Festival Register")Hirayama (1999), p.384. The register, consisting of 75 fascicles with subsequent lacunae, is noted for its extensive {{ill|Insect Damage|ja|虫損|12=draft}}. According to shrine tradition, it was compiled in [[1575]] (Tenshō 3), and among the names of Takeda retainers recorded therein, {{ill|Matsuki Awajimori|ja|末木家重|lt=Matsuki Awajimori|lt_ja=末木淡路守|12=draft}} (listed as “Ie-Chige”) is noted to have been active from the late Eirōku to the Tenshō period—retiring in Tenshō 9 and dying in Tenshō 15. Furthermore, both Amakawa Hyōbesuke and Amakawa Miyauchi-suke appear in the {{ill|Tenshō Jin-Go Petition|ja|天正壬午起請文|12=draft}}, which was submitted to the Tokugawa clan after the fall of the Takeda; this supports the shrine tradition that the register was compiled during the Tenshō period. == Miwa Shrine’s Taitei Kagura == During the spring festival, the {{ill|Taitei Kagura|ja|太々神楽|12=draft}} is performed in the shrine’s Kagura Hall within the precincts—during the evening ceremony and the following main festival—by members of the Miwa Shrine Kagura Preservation Society (all local parishioners). The repertoire includes a wide variety of dances, both maskless and masked, solo and small-group performances, with or without narrative elements. Among these are the Cleanse-the-Assembly Dance, Nation-Founding Dance, Four Pillars Dance, Descent Dance, Four Bows Dance, Group Dance, Sword Strike Dance, Preservation Deity Dance, National Orientation Dance, Fish Catching Dance, Sword Dance, Four Swords Dance, Treasure Ring Dance, Seed-Planting Dance, Great Serpent Dance, Evil-Illness Exorcism Dance, Fortune Change Dance, Ame-no-Iwato Dance, and Final Dance—a total of twenty surviving types. On the day of the festival, in the morning the {{ill|Urayasu Dance|ja|浦安の舞|12=draft}} is performed by young girls at the main shrine, after which the sacred spirit is transferred to the portable shrine which then departs toward Onoue. The Kagura continues until the portable shrine, having concluded its ritual at {{ill|Kinegami Shrine|ja|杵衡神社|12=draft}}, returns. According to the local tradition “On the Revival of This Kagura”, Miwa Shrine’s Kagura was revived when the main shrine building was reconstructed in [[1754]] (Hōreki 4) during the mid-Edo period. The “Kagura Twenty-Five Order” contained in the shrine documents is believed to date from the late Edo period, incorporating many elements of the old Ise-style order—including numerous maskless dances—which differ from the present repertoire. == See Also == *{{ill|Seichi junrei|ja|巡礼 (通俗)|12=draft}} * {{ill|Ōyamadera|ja|大山寺 (尾道市)|12=draft}} == References == {{reflist}} == Bibliography == * ''Hiroshima Encyclopedia'' (広島県大百科事典〈下巻〉). Period of {{ill|Emperor Keikō|ja|景行天皇|12=draft}} |main_shrine = {{ill|Nagare-zukuri|ja|流造|12=draft}} |alternative_names = |subsidiary = |festival = {{ill|March 15|ja|3月15日|12=draft}} |ritual = Yudate Ritual (February 8) |map = {{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=13|frame-align=center|frame-width=200}} }} {{ill|Miwa Shrine (Fuefuki City)|ja|美和神社 (笛吹市)|1=Miwa Shrine (Fuefuki City)|lt=Miwa Shrine|12=draft}} (美和神社) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in [[Japan]]. It is a [[Ninomiya (shrine)|Ninomiya]], or a second rank shrine in its province after the [[Ichinomiya]]. [[File:Miwa shrine Fuefuki-city.JPG|thumb|250px|Torii at Miwa Shrine (photo taken in April 2010)]] [[en:draft:Miwa Shrine (Fuefuki City)]] [[ja:美和神社 (笛吹市)]] [[ja:御袖天満宮]] [[sn:Miwa Shrine (Fuefuki City)]] [[File:Miwa shrine Fuefuki-city.JPG|thumb|250px|Miwa Shrine Torii (Photographed April 2010)]] '''Miwa Shrine''' (美和神社) is a {{ill|Shrine|ja|神社|12=draft}} located in {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|ja|山梨県|12=draft}} {{ill|Fuefuki City|ja|笛吹市|12=draft}}. It is a {{ill|Kokushi-Minaisha|ja|国史見在社|12=draft}}, and in {{ill|Kai Province|ja|甲斐国|12=draft}} it is known as {{ill|First Shrine|ja|一宮|lt=Second Shrine|lt_ja=二宮|12=draft}}, with its former shrine rank being {{ill|Prefectural Shrine|ja|県社|12=draft}}. == Deity == * {{ill|Ōmononushi|ja|大物主神|12=draft}} (Oomononushi-no-Kami) == Location == Miwa Shrine is situated in the eastern part of the {{ill|Kofu Basin|ja|甲府盆地|12=draft}} and enshrined in the Ninomiya district of the northwestern area. In ancient Kai Province, the early provincial capital ({{ill|Provincial Capital|ja|国府|12=draft}}) was located in {{ill|Kasuga Town, Fuefuki City|ja|笛吹市春日居町|12=draft}}, at the north-central edge of the basin, and is believed to have later been relocated to the vicinity of the national government office in {{ill|Misaka Town, Fuefuki City|ja|笛吹市御坂町|12=draft}}. The Misaka area is dotted with small to medium-sized burial mounds from the Kofun period—such as the {{ill|Kamekōdzuka Tumulus|ja|亀甲塚古墳|12=draft}} and {{ill|Baba Tumulus|ja|姥塚古墳|12=draft}}—as well as settlement ruins like the {{ill|Ninomiya Ruins|ja|二之宮遺跡|12=draft}}, and in ancient times, various governmental ruins and historic sites were spread throughout the area. Under the Ritsuryō system, the area was equated with Inoue Village in Yamanashi District, and the name “Ninomiya” is derived from its proximity to the national administrative office and Miwa Shrine. In the early modern period, Ninomiya Village was established, centered around Miwa Shrine. The shrine, located in the Ninomiya district, is designated as {{ill|Satomiya|ja|里宮|12=draft}}, while in the Oyama area to the east of Ninomiya stands {{ill|Yamamiya|ja|山宮|12=draft}} in the form of {{ill|Kinegami Shrine|ja|杵衡神社|12=draft}}. == History == It is generally believed that Miwa Shrine was enshrined by being invited from {{ill|Ōmiya Shrine|ja|大神神社|12=draft}} of {{ill|Yamato Province|ja|Yamato Province|12=draft}} ({{ill|Nara Prefecture|ja|奈良県|12=draft}}), which regards {{ill|Mount Miwa|ja|三輪山|12=draft}} as its shintai, and that after being transferred to the {{ill|Kinegami Shrine|ja|杵衡神社|12=draft}} in Onoe Village, it was newly relocated to Ninomiya. According to the texts “{{ill|Kai Kokashiki-ji|ja|甲斐国社記・寺記|12=draft}}” and “{{ill|Kai Kokushi|ja|甲斐国志|12=draft}}”, the shrine’s origins are said to date back to the time of {{ill|Emperor Keikō|ja|景行天皇|12=draft}}, when the provincial governor of Kai ({{ill|Provincial Governor of Kai|ja|甲斐国造|12=draft}}) and {{ill|Shio-umi Ashin|ja|塩海足尼|12=draft}} performed the enshrinement. The earliest historical record appears in an entry of “{{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|ja|日本三代実録|12=draft}}” dated June 8, [[863]] ({{ill|Jōgan era|ja|Jōgan|12=draft}} 5), which states that on that day Miwa Shrine was conferred the junior fifth rank and granted the title “Ninomiya” by {{ill|Emperor Ichijō|ja|一条天皇|12=draft}}. In the medieval period, it received veneration from the {{ill|Takeda clan|ja|武田氏|12=draft}}—the guardians of Kai—and in [[1479]] ({{ill|Bunmei era|ja|Bunmei|12=draft}} 11) the lord of {{ill|Shinano Province|ja|信濃国|12=draft}}’s {{ill|Saku District|ja|佐久郡|12=draft}}, the {{ill|Ōi clan|ja|大井氏|12=draft}}, invaded Kai; during this time Miwa Shrine also suffered from warfare. In the period of {{ill|Takeda Shigetora|ja|武田信虎|12=draft}}, the shrine was granted estates in {{ill|Manriki Village|ja|万力郷|12=draft}} in {{ill|Yamanashi District|ja|山梨郡|12=draft}} (present-day {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|ja|山梨県|12=draft}}), and in [[1557]] ({{ill|Kōji era|ja|Kōji (Muromachi period)|lt=Kōji|lt_ja=Kōji|12=draft}} 3) it received a charter from {{ill|Takeda Shingen|ja|武田信玄|lt=Takeda Harunobu|lt_ja=武田晴信|12=draft}} (Shingen), alongside {{ill|Asama Shrine (Fuefuki City)|ja|浅間神社 (笛吹市)|lt=Asama Shrine|lt_ja=浅間神社|12=draft}} (located in Ichinomiya, Ichinomiya Town, Fuefuki City), {{ill|Tamamoro Shrine|ja|玉諸神社|lt=Tamamoro Shrine|lt_ja=玉諸神社|12=draft}} in Kōfu City, and the Takeda clan’s tutelary shrine, {{ill|Takeda Hachiman Shrine|ja|武田八幡宮|12=draft}} (in {{ill|Nirasaki City|ja|韮崎市|12=draft}}), among others—exempting them from serving at Fuchū Hachiman Shrine (currently {{ill|Hachiman Shrine (Kōfu)|ja|八幡神社 (甲府市宮前町)|12=draft}} in Kōfu City). In June [[1565]] (Eiroku 8) a {{ill|Tachi (sword)|ja|太刀|12=draft}} offering was made by a retainer of {{ill|Takeda Yoshinobu|ja|武田義信|12=draft}}, the heir of the Takeda family, as recorded in the Miwa Shrine document “Kōshū Ninomiya Zōritchō”. According to “{{ill|Kōyō Gunkan|ja|甲陽軍鑑|12=draft}}”, in January of the preceding year [[1564]] (Eirōku 7) a retainer of Yoshinobu was punished for attempting a rebellion, and in the following year, [[1565]] (Eirōku 8), an incident occurred in which Yoshinobu himself was confined; however, from the records of the Zōritchō it is thought that the incident was uncovered in 1565 (Eirōku 8). Furthermore, in the following year [[1566]] (Eirōku 9), {{ill|Sanjō Consort|ja|三条夫人|12=draft}}—who was also the mother of Yoshinobu—offered armaments ({{ill|Armor|ja|具足|12=draft}}). On September 11, [[1573]] ({{ill|Genki era|ja|元亀|12=draft}} 4) immediately after the succession, {{ill|Takeda Katsuyori|ja|武田勝頼|12=draft}} ordered a prayer for enduring military fortune, and in [[1579]] ({{ill|Tenshō era|ja|天正|1=Tenshō (Momoyama period)|lt=Tenshō Era|12=draft}} 7) he imposed a prohibition. After the fall of the Takeda clan, in [[1582]] (Tenshō 10) prohibitions were issued by {{ill|Oda Nobunaga|ja|織田信長|12=draft}} and {{ill|Oda Nobutada|ja|織田信忠|12=draft}}, and in the following year [[1583]] (Tenshō 11) the shrine received a guarantee for its estates from {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|ja|徳川家康|12=draft}}, with the estates finally confirmed in [[1589]] (Tenshō 17) by a land survey conducted by {{ill|Inatadashi|ja|伊奈忠次|12=draft}}. During the era of Toyotomi-affiliated daimyō, the shrine received donations of estates from {{ill|Kato Mitsuyasu|ja|加藤光泰|12=draft}} and the {{ill|Asano clan|ja|浅野氏|12=draft}}. As a ritual, from the Sengoku period through early modern times a joint pilgrimage—known as the “Three-Shrine Onmiyuki”—was mandated. This ritual, performed at the Shingen Embankment ({{ill|Shingen Embankment|ja|信玄堤|12=draft}}) in {{ill|Kai City|ja|甲斐市|12=draft}}, involved the three shrines of Ichinomiya and Sannomiya; the summer onmiyuki was held on the third Ino day in April, and the winter onmiyuki on the second Ino day in November. During the Meiji period, with the prohibition of the three-shrine pilgrimage, the Yamamiya Onmiyuki (the Ninomiya Onmiyuki), which had been held on the first day of March, was rescheduled to April 15 and designated as the spring festival; although this event was interrupted for a time in the postwar era, it is now held on the first Sunday of April with the Taitei Kagura offered in dedication. Also, every February 8 the {{ill|Yudate Ritual|ja|湯立神事|12=draft}} is observed. Miwa Shrine’s Yudate Ritual, which is accompanied by the prayer dance of Sarutahiko, is the only surviving Yudate Ritual in the prefecture. According to a locally handed‐down document from 1826 (Bunsei 9), the Ninomiya Yudate was held separately on February 8—distinct from the Taitei Kagura held in mid‐March—and the dance of Sarutahiko is also recorded in {{ill|Uramihankuwa|ja|裏見寒話|12=draft}}. The shrine priesthood is provided by the Sakanai family, and {{ill|Sakanai Sōō|ja|坂名井聡翁|12=draft}} is known as a Kokugaku scholar. == Cultural Properties, etc. == [[File:Miwa-shrine Yutateshinji Kagura.JPG|thumb|250px|Prayer Dance of Sarutahiko during the Yudate Ritual (Photographed February 8, 2011)]] [[File:Miwa-shrine Yutateshinji A.JPG|thumb|250px|Ritual during the Yudate Ritual (Photographed February 8, 2011)]] [[File:Miwa-shrine Yutateshinji B.JPG|thumb|250px|Soaking bamboo leaves in boiling water and pouring it on worshippers (Photographed February 8, 2011)]] ; Important Cultural Properties (National Designation) * Sculpture ** Wooden Standing Statue of Ōmononushi – designated in [[1906]] (Meiji 39) on September 6; a work from the Heian period{{National Designated Cultural Properties Database|201|2937|Wooden Standing Statue of Ōmononushi}} (accessed May 19, 2017){{PDFlink|[https://www.city.fuefuki.yamanashi.jp/documents/607/5bf21d9faea4d.pdf Fuefuki City Cultural Properties Guidebook]}} – Fuefuki City, accessed December 23, 2019. ; Designated Tangible Cultural Properties of Yamanashi Prefecture * Crafts ** White Thread-Tied Armor (fragmentary) – designated in [[1986]] (Showa 61) on March 19; a work from the Nanboku-chō period{{Refnest|group="Notes"|Armor researcher Ichirō Miura has estimated, based on its manufacturing technique, that this armor dates from the period of {{ill|Takeda Nobunari|ja|武田信成|12=draft}} and {{ill|Takeda Nobuharu|ja|武田信春|lt=Nobuharu|lt_ja=信春|12=draft}}.Ichirō Miura, ''Resurrecting the Takeda Army: Its Armor and Military Attire'', Miyabari Publishing, May 28, 2007, pp. 7–13}} ** Vermilion Talisman and Red Thread Unarmored Armor with Accompanying Targe – designated in 1986 (Showa 61) on March 19; a legendary coming-of-age armor of {{ill|Takeda Shingen|ja|武田信玄|lt=Takeda Harunobu|lt_ja=武田晴信|12=draft}}{{Refnest|group="Notes"|However, Ichirō Miura notes that from its style this armor is a work of the Tenshō period—later than the time of Shingen’s coming-of-age—and that its manufacturing technique and design share commonalities with the armors of military commanders active under the Oda–Toyotomi regime (such as the gold small-talisman white thread unarmored armor of {{ill|Maeda Toshiie|ja|前田利家|12=draft}}, an Important Cultural Property held by the {{ill|Maeda Ikutoku Association|ja|前田育徳会|12=draft}}); he speculates that its actual user was either {{ill|Hideyasu Kawajiri|ja|河尻秀隆|12=draft}}, who governed Kai after the fall of the Takeda clan, or a person in his circle.Ichirō Miura, ''Resurrecting the Takeda Army: Its Armor and Military Attire'', Miyabari Publishing, May 28, 2007, pp. 13–19. Furthermore, the chiseled section on its left shoulder is thought to be a possible sword wound scar from Hideyasu’s demise.}} * Paintings ** Colored Panel Painting of the Thirty-Six Immortal Poets – designated in [[1965]] (Showa 40) on August 19; donated jointly in [[1563]] (Eirōku 6) by Takeda Shingen and Takeda Yoshinobu, father and son ; Prefectural Designated Intangible Folk Cultural Properties * Miwa Shrine’s Taitei Kagura – one wooden plaque and one plate of the “Kagura Twenty-Five Order” – designated in [[1981]] ({{ill|Showa era|ja|昭和|12=draft}} 56) on March 12; said to have originated during the {{ill|Genroku period|ja|元禄|12=draft}} In addition, the Sakanai family—the shrine’s priesthood ({{ill|Shrine Priest|ja|神主|12=draft}})—has preserved documents spanning from the medieval period to modern times, which were transferred to the {{ill|Yamanashi Prefectural Museum|ja|山梨県立博物館|12=draft}} in Heisei 21. === "Tenshō Nenchū Ninomiya Festival Register" === Miwa Shrine has inherited the "Tenshō Nenchū Ninomiya Festival Register" (also known simply as the "Festival Register")Hirayama (1999), p.384. The register, consisting of 75 fascicles with subsequent lacunae, is noted for its extensive {{ill|Insect Damage|ja|虫損|12=draft}}. According to shrine tradition, it was compiled in [[1575]] (Tenshō 3), and among the names of Takeda retainers recorded therein, {{ill|Matsuki Awajimori|ja|末木家重|lt=Matsuki Awajimori|lt_ja=末木淡路守|12=draft}} (listed as “Ie-Chige”) is noted to have been active from the late Eirōku to the Tenshō period—retiring in Tenshō 9 and dying in Tenshō 15. Furthermore, both Amakawa Hyōbesuke and Amakawa Miyauchi-suke appear in the {{ill|Tenshō Jin-Go Petition|ja|天正壬午起請文|12=draft}}, which was submitted to the Tokugawa clan after the fall of the Takeda; this supports the shrine tradition that the register was compiled during the Tenshō period. == Miwa Shrine’s Taitei Kagura == During the spring festival, the {{ill|Taitei Kagura|ja|太々神楽|12=draft}} is performed in the shrine’s Kagura Hall within the precincts—during the evening ceremony and the following main festival—by members of the Miwa Shrine Kagura Preservation Society (all local parishioners). The repertoire includes a wide variety of dances, both maskless and masked, solo and small-group performances, with or without narrative elements. Among these are the Cleanse-the-Assembly Dance, Nation-Founding Dance, Four Pillars Dance, Descent Dance, Four Bows Dance, Group Dance, Sword Strike Dance, Preservation Deity Dance, National Orientation Dance, Fish Catching Dance, Sword Dance, Four Swords Dance, Treasure Ring Dance, Seed-Planting Dance, Great Serpent Dance, Evil-Illness Exorcism Dance, Fortune Change Dance, Ame-no-Iwato Dance, and Final Dance—a total of twenty surviving types. On the day of the festival, in the morning the {{ill|Urayasu Dance|ja|浦安の舞|12=draft}} is performed by young girls at the main shrine, after which the sacred spirit is transferred to the portable shrine which then departs toward Onoue. The Kagura continues until the portable shrine, having concluded its ritual at {{ill|Kinegami Shrine|ja|杵衡神社|12=draft}}, returns. According to the local tradition “On the Revival of This Kagura”, Miwa Shrine’s Kagura was revived when the main shrine building was reconstructed in [[1754]] (Hōreki 4) during the mid-Edo period. The “Kagura Twenty-Five Order” contained in the shrine documents is believed to date from the late Edo period, incorporating many elements of the old Ise-style order—including numerous maskless dances—which differ from the present repertoire. == See Also == *{{ill|Seichi junrei|ja|巡礼 (通俗)|12=draft}} * {{ill|Ōyamadera|ja|大山寺 (尾道市)|12=draft}} == References == {{reflist}} == Bibliography == * ''Hiroshima Encyclopedia'' (広島県大百科事典〈下巻〉).
