{{ill|Kai Province|en|Kai Province|qid=Q858076|lt=Kai Province|1=Kai Province}}{{ill|Ichinomiya|en|Ichinomiya|qid=Q1656379|lt=Second Shrine|1=Ichinomiya}}
Former {{ill|Prefectural Shrine|ja|県社|1=Ken-sha|qid=Q90139226}}{{efn|Ken-sha|qid=Q90139226|lt=Ken-sha|1=modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prefectural Shrine|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 近代社格制度|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q712534}} |foundation = (trad.) Period of {{ill|Emperor Keikō|en|Emperor Keikō|qid=Q329723|lt=Emperor Keikō|1=Emperor Keikō}} |main_shrine = {{ill|Nagare-zukuri|en|Nagare-zukuri|qid=Q210684|lt=Nagare-zukuri|1=Nagare-zukuri}} |alternative_names = |subsidiary = |festival = {{ill|March 15|en|March 15|qid=Q2403|lt=March 15|1=March 15}} |ritual = Yudate Ritual (February 8) |map = {{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=13|frame-align=center|frame-width=200}} |location = {{ill|Fuefuki|qid=Q849434|1=Fuefuki}} |architecture_style = {{ill|nagare-zukuri|qid=Q210684|1=Nagare-zukuri}} }} {{ill|Miwa Shrine (Fuefuki City)|ja|美和神社 (笛吹市)|1=Miwa Shrine (Fuefuki City)|lt=Miwa Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Miwa Shrine (Fuefuki City)|13=User:Immanuelle/Miwa Shrine (Fuefuki City)|qq=}} (美和神社) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|qid=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine|1=Shinto shrine}} located in {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|qid=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}}. It is a [[:en:Ninomiya (shrine)|Ninomiya]], or a second Rank shrine in its province after the [[Ichinomiya]]. [[File:Miwa shrine Fuefuki-city.JPG|thumb|250px|Torii at Miwa Shrine (photo taken in April 2010)]] [[File:Miwa shrine Fuefuki-city.JPG|thumb|250px|Miwa Shrine Torii (Photographed April 2010)]] '''Miwa Shrine''' (美和神社) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|qid=Q845945|lt=Shrine|1=Shinto shrine}} located in {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|en|Yamanashi Prefecture|qid=Q132720|lt=Yamanashi Prefecture|1=Yamanashi Prefecture}} {{ill|Fuefuki|en|Fuefuki|qid=Q849434|lt=Fuefuki City|1=Fuefuki}}. It is a {{ill|Kokushi-Minaisha|ja|国史見在社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kokushi-Minaisha|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 社格|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Shakaku|qid=Q10444029}}, and in {{ill|Kai Province|en|Kai Province|qid=Q858076|lt=Kai Province|1=Kai Province}} it is known as {{ill|Ichinomiya|en|Ichinomiya|qid=Q1656379|lt=Second Shrine|1=Ichinomiya}}, with its former shrine Rank being {{ill|Prefectural Shrine|ja|県社|1=Ken-sha|qid=Q90139226}}{{efn|Ken-sha|qid=Q90139226|lt=Ken-sha|1=modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prefectural Shrine|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 近代社格制度|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q712534}}. == Deity == * {{ill|Ōmononushi|ja|大物主神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōmononushi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大物主}} (Oomononushi-no-Kami) == Location == Miwa Shrine is situated in the eastern part of the {{ill|Kōfu Basin|lt=Kōfu Basin|lt=Kofu Basin|ja|甲府盆地|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kofu Basin|qq=}} and enshrined in the Ninomiya district of the northwestern area. In ancient Kai Province, the early provincial capital ({{ill|Kokufu|en|Kokufu|qid=Q1629088|lt=Provincial Capital|1=Kokufu}}) was located in {{ill|Kasuga Town, Fuefuki City|ja|笛吹市春日居町|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga Town, Fuefuki City|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, at the north-central edge of the basin, and is believed to have later been relocated to the vicinity of the national government office in {{ill|Misaka Town, Fuefuki City|ja|笛吹市御坂町|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Misaka Town, Fuefuki City|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. The Misaka area is dotted with small to medium-sized burial mounds from the Kofun period—such as the {{ill|Kamekōdzuka Tumulus|ja|亀甲塚古墳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamekōdzuka Tumulus|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} and {{ill|Baba Tumulus|ja|姥塚古墳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Baba Tumulus|1=ubazukakofun|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q107655967}}—as well as settlement ruins like the {{ill|Ninomiya Ruins|ja|二之宮遺跡|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninomiya Ruins|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, and in ancient times, various governmental ruins and historic sites were spread throughout the area. Under the Ritsuryō system, the area was equated with Inoue Village in Yamanashi District, and the name “Ninomiya” is derived from its proximity to the national administrative office and Miwa Shrine. In the early modern period, Ninomiya Village was established, centered around Miwa Shrine. The shrine, located in the Ninomiya district, is designated as {{ill|Satomiya|ja|里宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Satomiya|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, while in the Oyama area to the east of Ninomiya stands {{ill|Yamamiya|ja|山宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamamiya|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in the form of {{ill|Kinegami Shrine|ja|杵衡神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kinegami Shrine|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. == History == It is generally believed that Miwa Shrine was enshrined by being invited from {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|en|Ōmiwa Shrine|qid=Q705542|lt=Ōmiya Shrine|1=Ōmiwa Shrine}} of {{ill|Yamato Province|en|Yamato Province|qid=Q907495|lt=Yamato Province|1=Yamato Province}} ({{ill|Nara Prefecture|en|Nara Prefecture|qid=Q131287|lt=Nara Prefecture|1=Nara Prefecture}}), which regards {{ill|Mount Miwa|en|Mount Miwa|qid=Q860627|lt=Mount Miwa|1=Mount Miwa}} as its shintai, and that after being transferred to the {{ill|Kinegami Shrine|ja|杵衡神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kinegami Shrine|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in Onoe Village, it was newly relocated to Ninomiya. According to the texts “{{ill|Kai Kokashiki-ji|ja|甲斐国社記・寺記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kai Kokashiki-ji|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}” and “{{ill|Kai Kokushi|ja|甲斐国志|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kai Kokushi|1=Kaikokushi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11577871}}”, the shrine’s origins are said to date back to the time of {{ill|Emperor Keikō|en|Emperor Keikō|qid=Q329723|lt=Emperor Keikō|1=Emperor Keikō}}, when the provincial governor of Kai ({{ill|Provincial Governor of Kai|ja|甲斐国造|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Provincial Governor of Kai|1=Kai no Kuni no Miyatsuko|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11577872}}) and {{ill|Shio-umi Ashin|ja|塩海足尼|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shio-umi Ashin|1=Shiomi no Sukune|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q100453532}} performed the enshrinement. The earliest historical record appears in an entry of “{{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|en|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|qid=Q1052981|lt=Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|1=Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku}}” dated June 8, {{ill|863|en|863|qid=Q25052|lt=863|1=863}} ({{ill|Jōgan era|ja|Jōgan|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jōgan era|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} 5), which states that on that day Miwa Shrine was conferred the junior fifth Rank and granted the title “Ninomiya” by {{ill|Emperor Ichijō|en|Emperor Ichijō|qid=Q449540|lt=Emperor Ichijō|1=Emperor Ichijō}}. In the medieval period, it received veneration from the {{ill|Takeda clan|en|Takeda clan|qid=Q1210114|lt=Takeda clan|1=Takeda clan}}—the guardians of Kai—and in {{ill|1479|en|1479|qid=Q6620|lt=1479|1=1479}} ({{ill|Bunmei era|ja|Bunmei|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bunmei era|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} 11) the lord of {{ill|Shinano Province|en|Shinano Province|qid=Q289250|lt=Shinano Province|1=Shinano Province}}’s {{ill|Saku District, Shinano|en|Saku District, Shinano|qid=Q7403130|lt=Saku District|1=Saku District, Shinano}}, the {{ill|Ōi clan|ja|大井氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōi clan|qq=}}, invaded Kai; during this time Miwa Shrine also suffered from warfare. In the period of {{ill|Takeda Nobutora|en|Takeda Nobutora|qid=Q1192628|lt=Takeda Shigetora|1=Takeda Nobutora}}, the shrine was granted estates in {{ill|Manriki Village|ja|万力郷|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Manriki Village|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in {{ill|Yamanashi District|ja|山梨郡|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamanashi District|qq=}} (present-day {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|en|Yamanashi Prefecture|qid=Q132720|lt=Yamanashi Prefecture|1=Yamanashi Prefecture}}), and in {{ill|1557|en|1557|qid=Q6595|lt=1557|1=1557}} ({{ill|Kōji era|ja|Kōji (Muromachi period)|lt=Kōji|lt_ja=Kōji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōji era|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} 3) it received a charter from {{ill|Takeda Shingen|en|Takeda Shingen|qid=Q276404|lt=Takeda Harunobu|1=Takeda Shingen}} (Shingen), alongside {{ill|Ichinomiya Asama Shrine (Fuefuki)|en|Ichinomiya Asama Shrine (Fuefuki)|qid=Q11557476|lt=Asama Shrine|1=Ichinomiya Asama Shrine (Fuefuki)}} (located in Ichinomiya, Ichinomiya Town, Fuefuki City), {{ill|Tamamoro Shrine|ja|玉諸神社|lt=Tamamoro Shrine|lt_ja=玉諸神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tamamoro Shrine|qq=}} in Kōfu City, and the Takeda clan’s tutelary shrine, {{ill|Takeda Hachiman Shrine|ja|武田八幡宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takeda Hachiman Shrine|1=Takeda-hachimangū|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11546131}} (in {{ill|Nirasaki, Yamanashi|en|Nirasaki, Yamanashi|qid=Q290326|lt=Nirasaki City|1=Nirasaki, Yamanashi}}), among others—exempting them from serving at Fuchū Hachiman Shrine (currently {{ill|Hachiman Shrine (Kōfu)|ja|八幡神社 (甲府市宮前町)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hachiman Shrine (Kōfu)|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in Kōfu City). In June {{ill|1565|en|1565|qid=Q6634|lt=1565|1=1565}} (Eiroku 8) a {{ill|Tachi|en|Tachi|qid=Q120676|lt=Tachi (sword)|1=Tachi}} offering was made by a retainer of {{ill|Takeda Yoshinobu|en|Takeda Yoshinobu|qid=Q837273|lt=Takeda Yoshinobu|1=Takeda Yoshinobu}}, the heir of the Takeda family, as recorded in the Miwa Shrine document “Kōshū Ninomiya Zōritchō”. According to “{{ill|Kōyō Gunkan|en|Kōyō Gunkan|qid=Q586111|lt=Kōyō Gunkan|1=Kōyō Gunkan}}”, in January of the preceding year {{ill|1564|en|1564|qid=Q6632|lt=1564|1=1564}} (Eirōku 7) a retainer of Yoshinobu was punished for attempting a rebellion, and in the following year, {{ill|1565|en|1565|qid=Q6634|lt=1565|1=1565}} (Eirōku 8), an incident occurred in which Yoshinobu himself was confined; however, from the records of the Zōritchō it is thought that the incident was uncovered in 1565 (Eirōku 8). Furthermore, in the following year {{ill|1566|en|1566|qid=Q6638|lt=1566|1=1566}} (Eirōku 9), {{ill|Sanjō Consort|ja|三条夫人|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sanjō Consort|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 三条の方|1=Lady Sanjō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q422018}}—who was also the mother of Yoshinobu—offered armaments ({{ill|Armor|ja|具足|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Armor|1=Gusoku (disambiguation)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11393749}}). On September 11, {{ill|1573|en|1573|qid=Q6678|lt=1573|1=1573}} ({{ill|Genki (era)|en|Genki (era)|qid=Q1145064|lt=Genki era|1=Genki (era)}} 4) immediately after the succession, {{ill|Takeda Katsuyori|en|Takeda Katsuyori|qid=Q662482|lt=Takeda Katsuyori|1=Takeda Katsuyori}} ordered a prayer for enduring military fortune, and in {{ill|1579|en|1579|qid=Q6709|lt=1579|1=1579}} ({{ill|Tenshō (Momoyama period)|en|Tenshō (Momoyama period)|qid=Q1145058|lt=Tenshō Era|1=Tenshō (Momoyama period)}} 7) he imposed a prohibition. After the fall of the Takeda clan, in {{ill|1582|en|1582|qid=Q6719|lt=1582|1=1582}} (Tenshō 10) prohibitions were issued by {{ill|Oda Nobunaga|en|Oda Nobunaga|qid=Q171411|lt=Oda Nobunaga|1=Oda Nobunaga}} and {{ill|Oda Nobutada|en|Oda Nobutada|qid=Q2446917|lt=Oda Nobutada|1=Oda Nobutada}}, and in the following year {{ill|1583|en|1583|qid=Q6726|lt=1583|1=1583}} (Tenshō 11) the shrine received a guarantee for its estates from {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|qid=Q171977|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu|1=Tokugawa Ieyasu}}, with the estates finally confirmed in {{ill|1589|en|1589|qid=Q6759|lt=1589|1=1589}} (Tenshō 17) by a land survey conducted by {{ill|Ina Tadatsugu|en|Ina Tadatsugu|qid=Q3387913|lt=Inatadashi|1=Ina Tadatsugu}}. During the era of Toyotomi-affiliated daimyō, the shrine received donations of estates from {{ill|Katō Mitsuyasu|en|Katō Mitsuyasu|qid=Q5354334|lt=Kato Mitsuyasu|1=Katō Mitsuyasu}} and the {{ill|Asano clan|en|Asano clan|qid=Q2659895|lt=Asano clan|1=Asano clan}}. As a ritual, from the Sengoku period through early modern times a joint pilgrimage—known as the “Three-Shrine Onmiyuki”—was mandated. This ritual, performed at the Shingen Embankment ({{ill|Shingen Embankment|ja|信玄堤|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shingen Embankment|1=Q4420072|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q4420072}}) in {{ill|Kai, Yamanashi|en|Kai, Yamanashi|qid=Q577309|lt=Kai City|1=Kai, Yamanashi}}, involved the three shrines of Ichinomiya and Sannomiya; the summer onmiyuki was held on the third Ino day in April, and the winter onmiyuki on the second Ino day in November. During the Meiji period, with the prohibition of the three-shrine pilgrimage, the Yamamiya Onmiyuki (the Ninomiya Onmiyuki), which had been held on the first day of March, was rescheduled to April 15 and designated as the spring festival; although this event was interrupted for a time in the postwar era, it is now held on the first Sunday of April with the Taitei Kagura offered in dedication. Also, every February 8 the {{ill|Yudate Ritual|ja|湯立神事|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yudate Ritual|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 湯立神楽|1=yudate kagura|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11563776}} is observed. Miwa Shrine’s Yudate Ritual, which is accompanied by the prayer dance of Sarutahiko, is the only surviving Yudate Ritual in the prefecture. According to a locally handed‐down document from 1826 (Bunsei 9), the Ninomiya Yudate was held separately on February 8—distinct from the Taitei Kagura held in mid‐March—and the dance of Sarutahiko is also recorded in {{ill|Uramihankuwa|ja|裏見寒話|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uramihankuwa|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. The shrine priesthood is provided by the Sakanai family, and {{ill|Sakanai Sōō|ja|坂名井聡翁|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sakanai Sōō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} is known as a Kokugaku scholar. == Cultural Properties, etc. == [[File:Miwa-shrine Yutateshinji Kagura.JPG|thumb|250px|Prayer Dance of Sarutahiko during the Yudate Ritual (Photographed February 8, 2011)]] [[File:Miwa-shrine Yutateshinji A.JPG|thumb|250px|Ritual during the Yudate Ritual (Photographed February 8, 2011)]] [[File:Miwa-shrine Yutateshinji B.JPG|thumb|250px|Soaking bamboo leaves in boiling water and pouring it on worshippers (Photographed February 8, 2011)]] ; Important Cultural Properties (National Designation) * Sculpture ** Wooden Standing Statue of Ōmononushi – designated in {{ill|1906|en|1906|qid=Q2049|lt=1906|1=1906}} (Meiji 39) on September 6; a work from the Heian period{{National Designated Cultural Properties Database|201|2937|Wooden Standing Statue of Ōmononushi}} (accessed May 19, 2017){{PDFlink|[https://www.city.fuefuki.yamanashi.jp/documents/607/5bf21d9faea4d.pdf Fuefuki City Cultural Properties Guidebook]}} – Fuefuki City, accessed December 23, 2019. ; Designated Tangible Cultural Properties of Yamanashi Prefecture * Crafts ** White Thread-Tied Armor (fragmentary) – designated in {{ill|1986|en|1986|qid=Q2430|lt=1986|1=1986}} (Showa 61) on March 19; a work from the Nanboku-chō period{{Refnest|group="Notes"|Armor researcher Ichirō Miura has estimated, based on its manufacturing technique, that this armor dates from the period of {{ill|Takeda Nobunari|ja|武田信成|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takeda Nobunari|1=Takeda Nobunari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q6640013}} and {{ill|Takeda Nobuharu|ja|武田信春|lt=Nobuharu|lt_ja=信春|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takeda Nobuharu|1=Takeda Nobuharu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q6640048}}.Ichirō Miura, ''Resurrecting the Takeda Army: Its Armor and Military Attire'', Miyabari Publishing, May 28, 2007, pp. 7–13}} ** Vermilion Talisman and Red Thread Unarmored Armor with Accompanying Targe – designated in 1986 (Showa 61) on March 19; a legendary coming-of-age armor of {{ill|Takeda Shingen|en|Takeda Shingen|qid=Q276404|lt=Takeda Harunobu|1=Takeda Shingen}}{{Refnest|group="Notes"|However, Ichirō Miura notes that from its style this armor is a work of the Tenshō period—later than the time of Shingen’s coming-of-age—and that its manufacturing technique and design share commonalities with the armors of military commanders active under the Oda–Toyotomi regime (such as the gold small-talisman white thread unarmored armor of {{ill|Maeda Toshiie|en|Maeda Toshiie|qid=Q1196817|lt=Maeda Toshiie|1=Maeda Toshiie}}, an Important Cultural Property held by the {{ill|Maeda Ikutokukai|en|Maeda Ikutokukai|qid=Q1333096|lt=Maeda Ikutoku Association|1=Maeda Ikutokukai}}); he speculates that its actual user was either {{ill|Kawajiri Hidetaka|en|Kawajiri Hidetaka|qid=Q6379555|lt=Hideyasu Kawajiri|1=Kawajiri Hidetaka}}, who governed Kai after the fall of the Takeda clan, or a person in his circle.Ichirō Miura, ''Resurrecting the Takeda Army: Its Armor and Military Attire'', Miyabari Publishing, May 28, 2007, pp. 13–19. Furthermore, the chiseled section on its left shoulder is thought to be a possible sword wound scar from Hideyasu’s demise.}} * Paintings ** Colored Panel Painting of the Thirty-Six Immortal Poets – designated in {{ill|1965|en|1965|qid=Q2650|lt=1965|1=1965}} (Showa 40) on August 19; donated jointly in {{ill|1563|en|1563|qid=Q6629|lt=1563|1=1563}} (Eirōku 6) by Takeda Shingen and Takeda Yoshinobu, father and son ; Prefectural Designated Intangible Folk Cultural Properties * Miwa Shrine’s Taitei Kagura – one wooden plaque and one plate of the “Kagura Twenty-Five Order” – designated in {{ill|1981|en|1981|qid=Q2437|lt=1981|1=1981}} ({{ill|Shōwa era|en|Shōwa era|qid=Q327567|lt=Showa era|1=Shōwa era}} 56) on March 12; said to have originated during the {{ill|Genroku|en|Genroku|qid=Q1325001|lt=Genroku period|1=Genroku}} In addition, the Sakanai family—the shrine’s priesthood ({{ill|Shrine Priest|ja|神主|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shrine Priest|1=Kannushi (disambiguation)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q15888735}})—has preserved documents spanning from the medieval period to modern times, which were transferred to the {{ill|Yamanashi Prefectural Museum|en|Yamanashi Prefectural Museum|qid=Q11469696|lt=Yamanashi Prefectural Museum|1=Yamanashi Prefectural Museum}} in Heisei 21. === "Tenshō Nenchū Ninomiya Festival Register" === Miwa Shrine has inherited the "Tenshō Nenchū Ninomiya Festival Register" (also known simply as the "Festival Register")Hirayama (1999), p.384. The register, consisting of 75 fascicles with subsequent lacunae, is noted for its extensive {{ill|Insect Damage|ja|虫損|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Insect Damage|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. According to shrine tradition, it was compiled in {{ill|1575|en|1575|qid=Q6688|lt=1575|1=1575}} (Tenshō 3), and among the names of Takeda retainers recorded therein, {{ill|Matsuki Awajimori|ja|末木家重|lt=Matsuki Awajimori|lt_ja=末木淡路守|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuki Awajimori|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (listed as “Ie-Chige”) is noted to have been active from the late Eirōku to the Tenshō period—retiring in Tenshō 9 and dying in Tenshō 15. Furthermore, both Amakawa Hyōbesuke and Amakawa Miyauchi-suke appear in the {{ill|Tenshō Jin-Go Petition|ja|天正壬午起請文|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenshō Jin-Go Petition|1=Q17218403|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q17218403}}, which was submitted to the Tokugawa clan after the fall of the Takeda; this supports the shrine tradition that the register was compiled during the Tenshō period. == Miwa Shrine’s Taitei Kagura == During the spring festival, the {{ill|Taitei Kagura|ja|太々神楽|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Taitei Kagura|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 神楽|1=Kagura|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q1348260}} is performed in the shrine’s Kagura Hall within the precincts—during the evening ceremony and the following main festival—by members of the Miwa Shrine Kagura Preservation Society (all local parishioners). The repertoire includes a wide variety of dances, both maskless and masked, solo and small-group performances, with or without narrative elements. Among these are the Cleanse-the-Assembly Dance, Nation-Founding Dance, Four Pillars Dance, Descent Dance, Four Bows Dance, Group Dance, Sword Strike Dance, Preservation Deity Dance, National Orientation Dance, Fish Catching Dance, Sword Dance, Four Swords Dance, Treasure Ring Dance, Seed-Planting Dance, Great Serpent Dance, Evil-Illness Exorcism Dance, Fortune Change Dance, Ame-no-Iwato Dance, and Final Dance—a total of twenty surviving types. On the day of the festival, in the morning the {{ill|Urayasu Dance|ja|浦安の舞|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Urayasu Dance|1=Urayasu no mai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11558194}} is performed by young girls at the main shrine, after which the sacred spirit is transferred to the portable shrine which then departs toward Onoue. The Kagura continues until the portable shrine, having concluded its ritual at {{ill|Kinegami Shrine|ja|杵衡神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kinegami Shrine|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, returns. According to the local tradition “On the Revival of This Kagura”, Miwa Shrine’s Kagura was revived when the main shrine building was reconstructed in {{ill|1754|en|1754|qid=Q7623|lt=1754|1=1754}} (Hōreki 4) during the mid-Edo period. The “Kagura Twenty-Five Order” contained in the shrine documents is believed to date from the late Edo period, incorporating many elements of the old Ise-style order—including numerous maskless dances—which differ from the present repertoire. == See Also == *{{ill|Seichi junrei|en|Seichi junrei|qid=Q123923583|lt=Seichi junrei|1=Seichi junrei}} * {{ill|Ōyamadera|ja|大山寺 (尾道市)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōyamadera|qq=}} == References == {{reflist}} == Bibliography == * ''Hiroshima Encyclopedia'' (広島県大百科事典〈下巻〉).
